speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
I desire to call the
attention of the Government to the delay or dereliction in bringing down returns to Orders of the House. I refer, first, to an order passed on the 24th March regarding correspondence between the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Quebec Harbour Commissioners with regard to dismissals. The 24th March is now about five weeks and a half past. The correspondence, I am informed, consists of only three letters. I do not know why it takes over five weeks to have three letters copied.
The next to which I call attention is an order for production of the correspondence relating to the appointment of Sir Robert Borden as Canadian representative at the International Disarmament Conference. This was moved for by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) and amended to meet a fuller requirement by myself. While there would be more than three letters in this correspondence, yet there would be very few, sufficient perhaps to occupy an hour in the copying. That has been three weeks delayed.
Then there was an order passed on the 3rd of April for correspondence passing between the late government and Hon. E. C. Drury respecting the activities of Hon. Manning Doherty in England. That correspondence consists of two letters, but the External Affairs Department apparently has not yet had time to copy them.
There was an order passed on the 27th of March regarding the dismissal of employees at the Sorel shipyards. That would take longer in preparation, but I cannot see why it would take any length of time. There has been no return as yet.
There are others, notably the correspondence relating to the deportation of Lee Holland, the order for the production of which was passed on the 24th of March. There has been no response as yet. It is a mystery to me why more than one or two days should have intervened before that return was brought down. I am quite aware there have been orders passed by this House that required lengthy correspondence with people far away to be brought up to date, gathered in, and copied, but these to which I called attention are not in that category at all. I do not know why any one of them should have been delayed more than two or three days, and I think they should be brought down at once.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I trust I may be permitted what may seem for a moment to be a digression, but which I consider to be a reasonable avenue of approach to my theme. I think it will be agreed that what we call the science of government trails far behind other sciences to-day, and this is due chiefly to its lack of facilities for experimentation. Not only are no means provided for scientific inquiry and experimentation with a view to improvement; but party government, as it has been conducted in the past, practically prohibits such. For instance, no allowance whatever is made for mistakes on the part of either

power to produce a great deal more than it is producing to-day if it were desired. It has the plant, the natural resources and the workmen; and it has need or demand for consumable goods. Consequently, if we accept the latter theory of credit, this country's credit is very excellent.
Those who control credit-which I claim is community power, and which to-day is in the hands of individuals-dictate, for instance, whether a capitalist shall produce or shall not produce. They dictate what we shall and shall not produce, and they also control the purchasing power of the nation. The purchasing power is affected very materially by such acts as the creation of new money and the recalling of loans, and these result in stopping the wheels of industry. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, the Brussels Conference, held some two years ago, when the financiers of the world were in session. Professor Gustave Cassels, who is now one of the representatives at Genoa, said of that conference that it had been deliberately brought about by the leaders of finance in order to increase the value of money. They wanted to bring about deflation so that money might increase in value, and the average citizen or consumer would be called upon to pay the difference, the financiers not being affected by the alteration.
In conclusion I desire to make a suggestion. Hon. members may not agree with me, but I ask them, at any rate, to consider what I have to say as a possibility. I think it is possible that we could handle our own credit and lend it to ourselves, thus becoming a lending rather than a borrowing nation. Let me instance what I mean. I understand that we have just floated $100,000,000 worth of bonds in the United States. Now, what is behind that issue? Is not the real wealth of Canada back of it? If the real wealth of Canada be considered by Wall Street as being sufficient security for that loan, why should not Canada consider that is is sufficient for her own credit and lend the money to herself? Moreover, if we had lent ourselves this money, we should save, to begin with, $2,500,000, which these brokers earned by one-half of a day's work. That, I suggest, is rather a high-wage. Those of us who have been speaking about the high wages paid workmen will surely have something to say about paying two and a half million dollars for a half day's work in order that we may obtain a loan.

Now, are there no means by which we can issue our own credit on the strength of our own real wealth, thus cutting out brokers' commissions and the interest that we have to pay? That is one of the questions which, I would suggest, is necessary to be investigated by such a committee as this resolution calls for. If there is no better way than that which we are following now, we shall set our teeth and go on to the -bitter end, dying gamely; but if there is any better way, it is only right that we should seek until we find it; and that is really all that my resolution calls for.
As I have said, I am not going to enter into a detailed discussion of a subject that I have been informed from many sources Parliament has no ears to listen to, even if I had the ability to do so. I merely put forward this resolution that a committee be appointed in order that they may collect the information necessary and bring it before the House, for it is of vital importance that we should be,fully seized of all information on the subject before we deal with our credit system further, as I believe we shall have to next session.
In conclusion, let me say that as far as I am aware there is no good reason why this resolution should not pass. Here are the reasons that I can think of why it should not pass:
In the first place, this resolution should not pass if we are already in possession of all the knowledge it is possible to have of the credit system which we as a Parliament have to do with, and which we delegate to the banks to handle.
In the second place, this resolution should not pass if this Parliament has nothing at all to do with the credit system. But I think we are very intimately interested in the subject when we are dealing in loans involving hundreds of millions of dollars, and when we place this great power in the hands of our banks by a vote of this House.
In the third place, this resolution should not be passed if we can deal with our banking system to better advantage without any knowledge of our credit system.
Those are reasons why we should not pass this resolution; there are no others. If we are sincere, as I believe we are, we want to get full knowledge of all subjects that come before this House. If we consider our credit system as fundamental to industry, if we believe that our credit is the actual wealth of Canada, if we believe

maintopic: ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY PROPOSED CONNECTION WITH THE EASTERN MAINE RAILWAY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is advisable that a branch line connecting the St. John and Quebec railway with the Eastern Maine railway be built as soon as financial conditions permit.
He said: [DOT] Mr. Speaker, my object in moving this resolution is to point out to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) and to the House a means of cutting down the operating expenses of the Canadian National Railways in the maritime provinces. I had this matter up with the then Minister of Railways in 1920, when I arranged a meeting between him, the president of the Eastern Maine Railway and the president of the St. John and Quebec Railway with a view to forwarding this proposition. The minister was very favourably inclined towards the project, in fact, later when it was discussed on the railway estimates, he expressed himself in these words, which will be found at page 3376 of Hansard, 1920.
Mr. J. D. Reid: I am familiar with the proposal to which my hon. friend (Mr. Caldwell) refers. About four years ago it was suggested that the Government should build that connecting line; it was shown that its construction
would residt in a great saving in the matter of traffic originating in the lower province and destined to the Eastern States. On account of the financial situation, action was delayed. There is no doubt that the construction of this line should be carried out.
A little further on he said:
I have no doubt at all that when we get back to normal conditions the Government will take up a scheme such as the one suggested and deal with these matters in the way that it is practically understood by the department and the railway officials that they should be carried out.
At the present time the Dominion Government is operating the St. John 4 p.m. and Quebec Railway under lease from the provincial government of New Brunswick. The province guaranteed the bonds for the construction of this road by the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, but that company having failed to carry the road to completion, the provincial government took the work over and to-day practically owns the line.
As I stated on a previous occasion, under the agreement between the provincial and Dominion governments it was provided that as the road was built in twenty-mile sections, the Dominion government should take it over and operate it as part of the Canadian National Railways. This has been done, something in the neighborhood of 160 miles having been constructed to date. For the year ending December 31, 1920, the operating deficit on this railway was $346,015.49. The agreement between the Dominion and provincial governments provides that the Dominion government shall have 60 per cent of the gross earnings to pay operating expenses, the other 40 per cent going to the province of New Brunswick to pay interest on the cost of construction. The 40 per cent of the gross earnings received by the province has failed to pay interest on the construction cost by $220,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the House may say: Well, this is not a very good showing on which to base a request that the Dominion government build a further extension of this road. But the reason for the deficit is that the road has never been completed as first contemplated. As originally planned the road was to run from St. John to Grand Falls, there to connect with the Transcontinental. Only part of that construction has been completed, there being still about 40 miles running from Centreville to Grand Falls to be built. On approaching the provincial government of New Brunswick at the head of a delegation some two years ago to see what promise we could get for

St. John and Quebec Railway
the completion of this northern section, we were informed that unless this connecting link between the St. John and Quebec Railway and the Eastern Maine Railway were built it would not be possible for the province to undertake the construction of the balance of the road as originally planned.
If the Government road is given no connection with the Eastern Maine Railway, then in all traffic to the United States we are confined to the Canadian Pacific. Now, there are two facts to be considered. The first is that two-thirds of the traffic which originates on the Canadian National Railways in the maritime provinces is destined to the United States; the second is that shipping to the United States by the Canadian Pacific we have to send our products over three railways. Every hon. member who has had any shipping experience knows that you pay a much higher freight rate to ship over two roads to a given point than over one, and if we have to ship over three roads, it makes it even more expensive. I believe it has been estimated that, due to this fact, we pay in excess freight yearly $100,000. The proposed link of railway I am advocating today is estimated to cost $1,000,000. Therefore, the saving in freight alone would pay for this piece of road in ten years. More than that, if this link is built it will enable the provincial government to construct the balance of the Quebec and St. John railway running north, which will open up that country and provide railway facilities for possibly the best section of New Brunswick, a section that has been settled a long time with the prospect of this road coming in to give them transportation facilities at a much earlier date than this.
This road was projected before the war. You will remember that last year the charter granting a subsidy of $6,400 a mile by the Dominion government was extended two years. It would have expired on 31 December last, but it was extended by this House on the request of the premier of New Brunswick. In the discussion that took place at that time it was shown why this road had not been constructed sooner. It was under construction when the war broke out. The Dominion government had agreed not only to give a subsidy of $6,400 a mile for every mile of this road that was completed, but it had also promised to build three very expensive bridges that would be necessary on this road, one on the northern section and two on the southern. Owing to war conditions and the fact that rail-

way material had advanced in price very rapidly, that labour had also advanced, and money was dear, this construction was not gone on with. The federal government at that time was under jure as great an obligation with regard to the completion of this road, so far as the building of bridges and a subsidy of $6,400 per mile was concerned, as the provincial government. The subsidy for the bridges has lapsed, and has not been renewed, but the subsidy of $6,400 per mile was renewed by this House last year. Now, in order to make it possible for the province to complete this road and for the government railways to operate economically, it is very necessary that the section I am advocating to-day should be built. At the present time the Eastern Maine Railway have a road surveyed, and I believe that construction is taking place, beginning this month from Houlton to Bancroft, Maine. The Eastern Maine Railway Company have agreed to build a spur from that road to the boundary line to meet the extension proposed by me to-day. They came to that agreement with the Minister of Railways [DOT]vo years ago, and they even agreed that if the Dominion government would build its section in 1921, they would build theirs in 1920, for the Minister of Railways, at that time Hon. Mr. Reid, asked these people, "What guarantee have we that you will build your end if we will build ours?" Hon. Mr. Reid promised the delegation, in my presence, that if he was Minister of Railways in 1921, he would bring in a bill for an appropriation to build this 22 miles of road. Last year, due to the heavy railway deficits, the stringency of the money market, and other conditions, the government did not see fit to go on with that work, although I think they could very well have done it at that time. To-day I think we are back pretty nearly to normal conditions so far as railroad construction is concerned. The price of labour and material has gone down, and I think the members of this House will agree that unemployment never was so acute as it is now. The building of this section would not only provide employment for the unemployed in the eastern provinces but, as I think I have clearly shown, though it would mean an initial outlay by the Government, it would pay for itself in ten years in the saving in freight alone, and the St. John and Quebec railway, the part now built and the balance that will be constructed if the section I am advocating is gone on with, instead of being a liability to the

St. John and Quebec Railway
Dominion government and the province of over half a million dollars a year, would become the best paying railway in eastern Canada, due to the fact that all the freight originating on the whole government system in the maritime provinces and destined for the United States would be routed over the St. John and Quebec Railway to get to this outlet. That would make the St. John and Quebec railway, instead of a deficit producer a revenue producer. I do not wish to take up the time of the House at any greater length, but I would urge upon the minister the advisability of the proposition I am putting before him at the present time.
Mr. RICHARD B. HANSON (York-Sunbury) : I do not wish to delay the House, but as this proposed road would start and end in my constituency, I should like to give the House the benefit of my views on the matter. This is not a new proposal by any means. I have no doubt that had it not been for the war this piece of railway construction would have been carried out by the government. The idea of building this section dates back to 1915, when Mr. Gutelius was the general manager of the Canadian Government railway lines. He was the originator of the idea, and it appealed to him because he felt the necessity of having an independent outlet for the Government lines into the New England states in order not to be obliged to turn over to the Canadian Pacific railway all the traffic originating on the government roads in the maritime ,provinces to reach the Boston and Maine railroad and through it to be distributed to the New England states.
I quite appreciate that this is not a very favourable time to ask the Government to embark on any new railway proposals, but I would suggest to the Minister of Railways that in the files of his department he will find, I am sure, data which will well repay his perusal, and which will, I believe, fortify and justify him when the time comes, as I have no doubt it will if he remains in power, in asking Parliament to build this branch line so that the Government railways may have an independent outlet into the New England states. 1. am not at all sure that it should be done through the Eastern Maine Railroad Company which has been referred to by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Caldwell). I hope that the company will be able to carry out its proposals, but I have very grave doubts as to their financial ability to do so. However, I would not like anything I
say in that connection to prejudice the mind of the minister against that particular company.
As to the principle involved, and as to the benefits that would be derived by the Government railways, I do not think there are any two opinions. While I have no doubt the minister will not be able to do anything this year, I would suggest to him that this is one of the construction proposals that he might well keep before hire is any construction programme that is undertaken in the immediate future. I arc sure that he would find the building of this section beneficial from a purely business standpoint to the department over which he presides.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. C. KENNEDY (Minister of Railways) :
maintopic: ST. JOHN AND QUEBEC RAILWAY PROPOSED CONNECTION WITH THE EASTERN MAINE RAILWAY
speechtext:
As my hon. friends have said, this matter has been before the House on former occasions. I am informed by the board of directors of the Canadian National railways that they have investigated this project, and while they are willing to admit that from the standpoint of interchange of traffic there is much that might be said in favour of further construction, yet they do not feel that the time is opportune to go on with it at the present time.
There was another point brought out by the mover of the resolution. The board is called upon to decide which of the railroads mentioned by my hon. friend would be the proper line to make connection with. As I understand there are five possible connections with two different railroads, and for the management of the National railways, or for the House, to commit themselves for the present time to either one might prejudice their views when they come to definitely decide which would be in the interset of the Canadian National lines. For the reason I think my hon. friend will agree that it is perhaps not desirable that we should state definitely at the present time with which line the connection should be made. However, I can assure my hon. friend that we will take the earliest opportunity of again bringing the matter before the attention of the Board of Directors. The attention of the board will be directed to what my hon. friend has said this afternoon, and I am sure that when the time is opportune they will give the matter every consideration. Under the circumstances I would therefore ask my hon. friend to withdraw the motion.

I merely want to assure the Minister of Railways that I hold no brief for the Eastern Maine Railway Company, and I realize the force of what my hon. friend for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has said. In this connection, Sir, it might be well if the Eastern Maine Company were willing to give the undertaking they did two years ago that they would build their section of the line this summer, and that our Government would agree to build theirs next summer. I may say further that I am not particular as to which road our government system makes connection with, so long as we get an outlet to the United States. So long as we can get connection with some road leading immediately to the centre of the eastern states, so that we may get an outlet for our traffic, I am not particular which road they connect up with.
I am pleased with the statement of the Minister of Railways although I cannot help recalling the promise I had from his predecessor both last year and the year before. We now have a new Minister of Railways and I would urge that he should give us something stronger than the mere assurance that the matter will be given due consideration. I would like the minister to give us an assurance that if the Eastern Maine, or any other railway company, is willing to build its share of the connection this year our Government would build our share next year-I think he might well go that far. I repeat that I am not particular which of the American roads he connects with; I certainly would prefer to leave that to the judgment of the board of management of the National Railways because they are in a much better position to decide what is feasible than I am. We desire this connection not only because of the outlet it will give to the centres of the eastern states but also because it will open up a splendid tract of country in our own province to the north which has been settled to some extent owing to the prospect of this road coming in at an early date.
I hope the minister will give an assurance that he will connect with an American road which will provide the necessary facilities.

That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the fact that the present federal Elections Act disfranchises a person who moves his residence from one electoral district to another during the two months previous to the issuing of writs for an election, action should be taken to amend said Elections Act, Article twenty-nine, paragraph C, so as to preserve the right of said elector to vote either in one or the other electoral district.

Elections Act
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it necessary to support this resolution with a long speech. Its purpose is so evident that it will suffice, I am sure, to bring it to the attention of the Government and the House to ensure its adoption. It deals with an obvious omission in the present federal Elections Act which seems to have escaped the attention of the last Parliament, but which the practice of the general elections of 1921 has made very clear, and demonstrated to be very annoying. According to the provisions of the present electoral law, adopted in 1920, a person who happens to move his residence during the two months preceding the issuing of writs is virtually disfranchised, and the law offers no way to reserve his right to vote. At least this is the condition that obtains in provinces, like Quebec, where new lists require to be prepared at every election. If you turn to paragraph 29 of that electoral law you will find that the qualifications for an elector are: (a) Must be a British subject by birth or naturalization; (b) Must be of the full age of twenty-one years; and (c) Must have "ordinarily resided in Canada for at least twelve months and in the electoral district wherein such person seeks to vote for at least two months immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election." That seems a very simple provision, but you will understand at once, Mr. Speaker, that a person who happens to move during that period of two months cannot qualify in the new riding to which he has transferred his residence because he has not lived there two months. On the other hand he cannot safeguard his right to vote in the old riding either, because he has not been there during the required full period before the issuance of the writs.
This applies both to the rural constituencies and city ridings, but cases which are very scarce in the rural parts of the country can be very numerous in city ridings. The last election was held on 6th December, and writs were issued some time in October. October first is moving day in large cities like Montreal. It happened to fall within this two months specified by law, and, by that omission, persons who should have had the right to vote, who merely happened to move their residences a few blocks in some instances, perhaps only across the street, from one riding to another, were actually disfranchised. A much greater number retained the right
to vote, in spite of the law, simply because no demand was made to have their names struck off the lists, but if such a demand had been made, the revising officer would have had to comply with the law and strike their names from the list. When the candidates become keener to the possibilities of this election law, if it remains as it is, in a city like Montreal alone thousands of voters could be disfranchised, if the election happened to be held in May or in October, the two moving dates in large cities. In order to leave no doubt in the minds of hon. members as to the effect of this statute, I should like to place on Hansard the opinion of no less an authority than Colonel Biggar, Chief Electoral Officer of the Dominion. During the last election he had to give decisions in cases similar to the one I have referred to, and in every case he authorized the statement that the law disqualified such persons, and gave instructions to the registrar and revising officers accordingly. When I placed this resolution on the Order Paper I wrote him asking his opinion, and his reply reads, in part, as follows:
During the election campaign I received a large number of inquiries on this point, and in the later edition of the Election Instruction (31st December 1921) prepared for the by-elections at which the procedure was considerably different from that followed at the general election, I made an addition to paragraph 137, as appears by the copy of these later Instructions which I also enclose. This addition further emphasises the undoubted effect of the provisions of the statute on the point.
I have here the election instructions prepared for the by-election of a new minister, and here is the addition which Colonel Biggar refers to in his letter. It will be found on page 48, section 137:
The effect of the statutory provisions on the subject of residential qualification is that everyone whose residence has been out of Canada during the year immediately preceding the date of the issue of the writ, and everyone who has changed his place of residence in Canada from one electoral district to another within the two months before that date is disqualified from voting.
The most remarkable feature about this is that if the elector happens to move after the issue of the writ then he can retain his right to vote in the electoral district where he has resided before that date, but if he happens to be unlucky enough to move at the very moment-that is at one of the sixty days preceding the issue of the writ-then he cannot qualify in the new riding, and he is bound to be disfranchised, if proper application is made to strike out his name. I think there
Elections Act

can be no doubt, after the authority I have just given, as to the effect of the present law.
This resolution does not specify any remedy. If I were to give my humble opinion, I think there should be a provision to allow the voter to retain his vote in the old riding, where he resided before he moved, and not in the new riding where he has moved his residence, because, in the latter case, the door would be opened to many misunderstandings and frauds. But I am not stressing that point. Earlier in the session the Government led the House to understand, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Bagot (Mr. Mar-cile), that the electoral law would be amended in some way. My opinion is that the act with which I am dealing would stand amendment on more than one point. I consider that the theory of allowing these lists to be revised just previous to the election may seem very equitable, but its practice is full of danger and may lead to abuses, and even to frauds of the worst kind. I think the whole system of preparing electoral lists at fixed dates during the time of peace-so to describe the period between electoral campaigns- is much better than the present practice. If we are to retain the present law, I say we should, at least, remedy the evil referred to in my resolution. It is altogether unfair to have a law which allows an individual voter to qualify at the last moment for an election, when this same law will disfranchise that voter simply because he happened to move at a certain date from one electoral district to another. I trust that when the occasion arises the Government will consider this matter. I would ask the House to accept the resolution in its present form. It is not contentious, and it only embodies the expression of a wish. I, therefore, beg to move, seconded by Mr. Prevost, the resolution standing in my name.

Mr. Speaker, It is with pleasure that I support the motion of the member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) because I consider it points out a rather serious omission in the Elections Act, a deficiency which should be remedied immediately and an amendment to the act brought down at this present session. By enacting that a person's name cannot be inscribed on the voters' list unless he has resided in the division where he wishes to vote, for at least two months previous

to the issuing of the writs, hundreds of persons are, as a natural consequence, disfranchised, and it is always a serious matter to disfranchise a citizen.
I admit, the question is of special interest to large cities which comprise numerous electoral districts where citizens often move from one district to another, but it is also important to small towns and rural parts. With reference to the last general elections, those who find fault are not so much the candidates who were returned by large majorities, but the people who bitterly regretted, and are still sore of having been deprived of their vote.
I mentioned that the question was an important one for the rural districts, and I believe it to be so. I am aware that the act allows a voter, even on election day, if his name is not on the list, to register his vote. However, he must be in a position to swear that he possesses all the qualifications prescribed by the act. Now, amongst these qualifications is to be found the one which we are at present discussing and which requires of a person, in order that he may exercise his franchise in an electoral district, to reside in such district for two months previous to the issuing of election writs; so that, notwithstanding this clause in the act which seems to open up a wide door to the voters who are not registered on the list and to enable them to make use of their right to vote, the omission which we pointed out would prevent the voter from exercising such franchise. I therefore deem it advisable to submit the question to this House and we have reason to hope that the Government will bring down an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act, such as mentioned in the motion of the member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) and which will be in the whole country's interest.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the House the benefit of my experience in this regard, and it will, perhaps, be a surprise to some of the members. I am thoroughly in accord with the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Rinfret). I am not sure that such a provision is required in the rural districts, because moving and shifting about in rural parts of the country is perhaps, not very great. When, however, we came to make a canvass in my riding in the last election, we found that between fifteen and twenty per cent of those whose names were on the list could not be found in the riding. Those people had moved, and, by moving,

Elections Act
they had opened the way, if any person had desired to be corrupt, to having all their names voted. Furthermore, a man is deprived of his vote, because he has moved, say from one side of Spadina avenue, in my city, to the other; that is, if he moves merely across the street, he is disfranchised. The only fact which I want to bring to the attention of the House is this, that, in a large city like Montreal or Toronto, many people otherwise entitled to vote are disfranchised on account of moving their residence immediately prior to an election. Perhaps, the percentage is greater in Toronto than in Montreal, because houses in Toronto are rented on a monthly tenancy basis, and in my riding between fifteen and twenty per cent of the people were disfranchised under the present act.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to approve the resolution also, because I know, even in rural or semirural places, many worthy citizens who were deprived of the privilege of voting at the last election under the law as it then stood and still stands. Therefore, a change is very desirable.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the matter referred to in the resolution of the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) is one worthy of consideration. It was considered when the present Dominion Franchise Act passed the House. Our difficulty then was our difficulty now, namely, to find a remedy. The same question came up in this House in 1897, when there was a discussion on the subject; and it was then felt, as it was felt two years ago, that probably less difficulty would arise from leaving the law in its present position than if we were to seek to change or amend it. The question arose more particularly in 1897 in regard to school teachers and, I think, also in regard to Methodist ministers. School teachers, particularly in Ontario in the rural sections, change their places very frequently; the ministers of some of our churches also change their residences periodically; and in many cases the teacher or the minister was disqualified simply by reason of the change. Then, in cities, it always occurs that men and women will move from one division to another. Nobody, however, has yet suggested a proper remedy for this condition of affairs. If you permit men, who have actually moved away from a riding, to come back and vote you may be opening a door
to the payment of expenses and to bringing voters from all parts of Canada, and that was looked upon as a great objection, both in years gone by and in the discussion that took place in this House two years' ago. But it is certainly a hard thing that any large body of our citizens should be disfranchised simply by reason of the fact that they have changed their residences immediately prior to the issue of an election writ. There may be something in the suggestion of my hon. friend that they could be permitted to vote in the place in which they formerly resided, but that would not, I believe, cure the evil for men and women who had moved to any great distance. Men from Ontario, from Quebec, go West, and these men would certainly be disfranchised; but the greatest hardship, I think, takes place in cities where a voter moves irom one division to another, but still remains practically in the same municipality. The motion is one well worthy of consideration, and I only wish the hon. member for St. James had suggested something like a remedy for the difficulty. I agree with him that when the Franchise Act comes up for amendment or consideration, this is a matter that should be considered.

Mr. Speaker, I take it, from the expression of opinion on both sides of the House, that there is no objection to accepting the resolution of the hon. member for St. James. As has been stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie), perhaps, the difficulty is to find a ready remedy. Of course, the first and natural impulse with every one is that he wants to have the right to vote, and after having the right to vote, he has some predilection for one place or another. The natural and most effective place for one to vote in is where he resides or where he proposes to reside for some time to come. The basic philosophy of the right to vote or the purpose of voting is that a person has a right to select a representative in Parliament; and if a man who lives in Montreal finds that he is moving to Toronto, he says: "Well, you may give me a vote in Montreal; but I am leaving Montreal; I am going to live in Toronto, and, after this I want to put myself in touch with the representative of the city in which I am going to live." To allow that man the right to vote in Montreal would not satisfy him, because he wants to have a representative in the city or province in which he goes to reside. It is more difficult to find a remedy for the situation of
Elections Act

that man. It is a simple proposition to legislate or to amend the act so as to leave with the man the right to vote where he is qualified and where he resides, so to amend the act that his right to vote shall continue for the first election that may take place after he has left that particular residence. It is not, however, so easy to furnish machinery by which you qualify him to vote in any other part of Canada to which he might move. I have not been able to come to any definite conclusion, but the only thing that suggests itself to me as practical in a case of that kind, would be that he might be permitted to vote on the certificate of the chief electoral officer. A man living in New Brunswick, for instance, might satisfy the Chief Electoral Officer that he was fully qualified to vote in any riding in Canada, and on going, say, to British Columbia, he could get from that officer a certificate under seal which, on presentation to any presiding officer in the latter province, would give him the right to vote at the first election thereafter. It is possible that some such machinery as that might meet the case. The other case is far less difficult, and if a voter were given the right to come back and vote where he resided, I do not think there would be any room for hardship. Most of these cases arise in the cities, and the matter of travelling one way or the other would not be very important. As has been suggested, many of these moves are merely across a street or alleyway, and it really does not make very much difference. It is quite likely, and I believe almost certain, that this matter will be dealt with and a proper remedy provided.
The hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), referred to our present franchise law, and the law as it stood years ago. Personally I think that the old franchise system was better. When we entered Confederation in 1867 the provincial franchise was adopted all round. In every province then in Confederation, members were elected to this House, I understand, under the local law, and that continued until 1885 or 1886, when a Dominion franchise was adopted by legislation of this Parliament. At that time officers, who were entitled revising officers, were appointed to prepare the lists in all the provinces. That practice was observed until 1898, when by common consent-I was not in the House then, but I understand there was no objection at all from either side-Parliament went back to the old condition and once more adopted the provincial franchise.

That continued down to the election of 1917, which was the first Dominion election since the reinstitution of the provincial franchise, at which members were returned to this Parliament under a Dominion system. The election of 1917 and the election of 1921 were both held under Dominion franchise. But the very large majority of the elections in Canada sirce Confederation have been held under the local law. In our own province we have what I regard as ideal conditions in regard to the franchise. Our lists are revised every year whether there is an election or not. On the 27th of April of each year the lists are closed and are ready for any election that might be called. Of course, they are not now used in Dominion elections; they are subject to certain additions and subtractions before they can serve the purposes of a Dominion election. I should have no hesitation whatever in recommending ours as a general system for Dominion elections. I am not speaking for the Government, but solely for myself, but in my judgment it would be the ideal practice for every province in Canada to have the lists prepared every year so that they might be ready at any time an election might be held. The expense, in our province at any rate, is not considered any objection at all. As a matter of fact, there is no great expense involved in preparing these lists every year.
However, the matter with which we shall have to deal in this connection will be simply the introduction of some slight amendment to secure the right to the voter to come back and vote where he resides, or otherwise to carry the franchise with him. There must be some such certificate as I have mentioned that he could carry with him so as to enable him to vote at the first Dominion election held after he has received it. I think the resolution of the hon. member is quite timely and I am sure the House will be pleased to deal with the matter when it comes up.

I think we are all agreed that every Canadian citizen eligible to vote should have the right to do so, and the mere fact that a man is forced sometimes, by circumstances beyond his control, to go to another constituency should not penalize him and prevent him from exercising the franchise as a Canadian citizen. I can readily understand that the provision that has been incorporated in the Election Act on this point has some basis in reason. It may have been placed there to make sure that no

Income Tax Act
individual would vote twice. But we are told by various hon. members that it appears to infringe upon the rights of voters more in the cities than anywhere else. In the rural districts very few people are penalized in this respect by moving; but in the cities, where people are continually on the move, it may be a great hardship, and I can see that there is likely to be some difficulty, no matter what you may do, to remedy the existing law. We do find, however, that in the resolution No. 12, relating to proportional representation and the alternative vote, there is a safeguard not only to the man who wishes to exercise his franchise, but also to the public interests of Canada, and I believe that when this subject is brought before the House and we have time to study it carefully we shall be able to remove a great many of the electioneering difficulties that at present exist. In this connection, I might refer to proportional representation in the cities. Under proportional representation I understand that no matter where a man may reside in the city, or whether he changes from one district to another within the pale of the city, he still has the right to vote; and I think that when that system comes up for consideration it will be time enough to indicate the benefits to be derived by the removal of a great many of the difficulties and anomalies of the Franchise Act. By the adoption of a proper system then we shall be able to ensure, not only to the individual who votes at an election, but also to collective bodies of voters, in the actual returns of men to this Parliament, a fair proportion of representation for every constituency. If it is necessary to change the existing law for rural districts, well. and good. But as we have been told that the great majority of inequalities that result from the present law are to be found in the cities, and as these inequalities can be finally removed only when we have a system under which every man will have the right to exercise the franchise under a city list rather than under a list in an electoral division, I believe that action should be delayed until the question of proportional representation is before the House for consideration.
Motion agreed to.

INCOME TAX ACT 1917 PROPOSED AMENDMENT RESPECTING ALIENS
speechtext:
That, to the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending- the Income Tax Act, 1917, as
amended toy subsequent acts by providing that there shall be paid upon the annual income of all aliens, not being residents of Canada, who are employed in Canada or derive income for services rendered in Canada S per cent upon all such incomes exceeding one thousand dollars.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution is not of a particularly compulsory character, because it simply suggests that "the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act, 1917." It is quite possible that many hon. members do not quite grasp the true meaning of this resolution, and therefore I desire first of all to point out why it has been introduced.
Prior to November, 1921, the Income Tax Act of the United States was practically the same as our Income Tax Act, giving similar exemptions to married and unmarried men and fixing the rate of taxation at the same rate on all those earning incomes in the United States whether resident in that country or elsewhere. But in November of last year Congress amended the Income Tax Act and made section 210 to read as follows:
That, in lieu of the tax imposed by section 210 of the Revenue Act of 1918, there shall be levied, collected, and paid for each taxable year upon the net income of every individual a normal tax of 8 per centum of the amount of the net income in excess of the credits provided in section 216 : provided, that in the case of a citizen or resident of -the United States the rate upon the first $4,000 of such excess amount shall be 4 per centum.
The exemption provided for in section 216 subsection (e) is as follows:
In the case of a non-resident alien individual or of a citizen entitled to the benefits of section 262, the personal exemption shall be only $1,000, and he shall not be entitled to the credit provided in subdivision (d).
But an American citizen is entitled to an exemption of $2,500 or $2,000.
This Act of Congress does not expressly mention Canadians, but there are no other non-resident aliens that I know of working in the United States. There may be some from Mexico, but those need not be taken into account.
The result is distinctly to the disadvantage of Canadians. Take the concrete case of the county of Welland that I have the honour to represent-and I know the same thing prevails in the county of Essex, and no doubt in the county of Lincoln and in every other constituency bordering on the international boundary line-Canadian citizens working in the United States-and there are at least 400 working at Niagara
Income Tax Act

Falls, New York, and Buffalo-if they have an income of $5,000, whether married or unmarried, their exemption is only $1,000, and they are taxed 8 per cent on the balance. In contrast with that the American citizen is allowed an exemption of $2,500 if he is a married man or a man with dependents, and he is taxed at the rate of only 4 per cent on the balance of his income.
Our law makes no distinction between Americans and Canadians. For instance, a United States citizen working in Canada is granted an exemption of $1,000 if he is an unmarried man, and he is taxed 4 per cent on the balance of his income; if he is a man with a family or other dependents, he is allowed an exemption of $2,000 and is still taxed only 4 per cent on the balance.
Now, as a rule I am not inclined to favour the adoption of retaliatory measures, but it seems to me that in so far as this Act of Congress affects Canadian citizens, it works a very grave injustice. Although a good many of our citizens work in the United States and live in Canada, it must not be forgotten that so far as our border constituencies are concerned there are just as many United States citizens working in Canada and living in their own country. Therefore, I claim that unless Congress remove this discrimination and make their law the same as our Income Tax Act, we should do our duty and place the same burdens on United States citizens that are now imposed on our citizens by this discriminatory legislation.
I have a letter from the president of a large manufacturing concern at Niagara Falls, Ontario, and I should like to place his views on Hansard. He is a United 'States citizen, and he writes as follows:
I am pleased to note that you have handled this matter in a very fair and reasonable way. We certainly trust that the problem can be solved without retaliatory legislation, although it is manifestly evident that such legislation should be taken by Canada if the situation cannot be corrected in any other way. We think that the move which you are taking may help to bring the seriousness of the situation before the United States Government.
As we have written, we are doing everything possible in the way of soliciting pressure from as many sources as possible to have this corrected and we have made the situation known to a large number of senators and representatives in Washington.
The situation is serious and aggravating to all manufacturers along the border and a great hardship to many employees of such manufacturers.
There is practically nothing more to be said about this subject. What I want is

that Parliament should approve of this resolution, which will fortify the Government in saying to the United States Congress, "We have the authority of Parliament to pass retaliatory legislation if we choose to do so, but we hope that you will consider it in the best interests of friendly relations and in the best interests of the people who are working on the two sides of the international boundary line to amend your law so as to make it conform with the law of Canada. In default of your doing so, it is quite possible that we may be forced by Parliament to pass retaliatory legislation that will place the same burden of taxation on your citizens working in Canada as is imposed on our citizens working in the United States." That is what I want this Parliament to do, and that is what I think this Parliament should do, irrespective of the friendly relations which now exist and have existed for so many years between the United States and Canada, and which I trust will continue to exist for many more years to come. I think it is our duty to stand by our own citizens and see that they are properly protected and safeguarded in regard to such legislation as this that has been passed in the United States. We hope of course, that conditions may be such in the near future that this burdensome taxation may be done away with, but it is in existence yet, and in all probability will remain in existence for several years to come-longer than we would like. That being so, I ask Parliament to approve of this resolution so that the Government may with the authority of Parliament say to the United States: "Unless you change your legislation and give our citizens the same rights that we accord to American citizens we will be bound to pass retaliatory legislation-it is a harsh term perhaps-"
