speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: INCOME TAX ACT 1917 PROPOSED AMENDMENT RESPECTING ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not quite certain from the terms of the resolution until I heard the address of the hon.

Old Age Pensions
member for Welland (Mr. German) just what he had in mind. I was aware of the legislation, though not in any detailed way, that gives rise to his resolution, that is to say, the legislation introduced in November last in the United States legislatures. To that legislation we in Canada cannot take exception from our special standpoint; it is legislation that is applicable everywhere; it is not discriminatory against our country, nor is its purpose to deflect the course of domestic policy in Canada. Nevertheless, it is legislation that of itself invites retaliatory action; it is legislation against which another country can protect itself only by retaliatory action. If the United States chooses to place upon the citizens of this country and of countries other than itself, earning money within its borders a burden beyond that borne by its own citizens, there is only one thing, it appears to me, for the neighbouring nation to do, and that is to act in a similar way. Otherwise, it places its own citizens at a disadvantage as compared with those across the line. Consequently, this would appear to me to be a timely resolution and one well worthy of the consideration of the Government and of this House.
There is, however, a class of legislation to which I think we in Canada can take just exception. It is that class of legislation which is directed not against all outside nations equally, but directed solely against ourselves, legislation designed to deflect the course of domestic policy within this country. There have been efforts made in recent times to have such legislation passed by the United States. I fear those efforts have been, or appear now to be, more or less successful. Such does not seem to me to be a course of policy designed to foster and improve the good relations that have subsisted between us for so many years. At the same time, if it is the course of policy that in their best judgment they see fit to adopt, it will be one that will have to be met in our country, not in a spirit of antagonism, not in a spirit wanting in friendship, but in a spirit of stern and immovable self-reliance.
I have pleasure, indeed, in offering commendation to the hon. member for Welland, and I hope that his suggestions will receive at the hands of the Government serious and sympathetic consideration.
Motion agreed to.

That, in the opinion of this House, the Dominion Government should consider the advisability of devising ways and means for the establishment of a system of old age pensions in Canada.
He said (Translation) : At the outset, Mr. Speaker, allow me to urge upon this House the desirability of legislation enabling the Government to grant a pension to old men. In so doing so, I am impelled by a deep sense of humanity and justice. Indeed, having for the last twenty-five years resided in the city of Hull,-an essentially industrial centre,-I have been able, more than any one else perhaps, and many a time, to realize that a great number of workmen after having spent the best part of their lives in factories and worn themselves out, become, in their old age a burden to their children, unless they seek refuge in a poor house. Is it not a painful sight, Mr. Speaker, to see these old employees, after contributing their share towards their country's welfare and development, after labouring for thirty, forty, nay fifty years to enrich others, once they have expended the whole of their assets,-for their physical fitness is truly an asset to them,-the moment they are disabled, worn out by age and work, reduced to poverty. I say that it is the duty of the state to assist these old men by paying them a pension in the form of annuities or endowment. Some might perhaps object that these men should have economized and laid aside their savings whilst they were young; but every member of this House knows perfectly well that their salaries are never sufficient to allow savings, because wages paid are always based on the cost of living. The following is an illustration. During the unfortunate war just ended, workmen obtained an increase of wages because the cost of living was increasing continually, and now the war is over, employers insist on a reduction in wages because, according to them, the cost of living has been reduced. It is therefore a well established fact that wages are fixed by the cost of living. We figure out how much it costs a workingman to live and support a family of five or six children, and the result of this calculation determines the salary he shall receive. How can he economize when he is paid just enough to provide his family with the strict necessities of life? let, the working man is entitled, as well as the rich man, to some comfort in this world. The working man

Old Age Pensions
has a heart, he loves his children as much as the rich man loves his own, and he would like to give them better means than he has himself had for the battles of life. How can he attain this end with such meagre wages as two or three dollars a day? -I especially refer to the working man, because it is he who would benefit the most from such a Pensions Act, but it should be fully understood that all those who attain the age, say of 65 years, man or woman, and are in need, whatever may have been their trade or business, would benefit from such a pension, provided they had been honest citizens.
Now, Mr. Speaker, allow me to discuss the question from another point of view. You know how the late war has expanded the outlook of classes in this country; the farmers movement has spread, the labour movement has developed; and the labourer now says to himself, and not without cause, that if he has been useful during the war, if he has participated in destroying German militarism and in saving civilization, he is fully entitled to some reward. Truly, amongst all the classes of society, it is the labouring class which supplied the most men and which was the first to respond to the call to arms, and now that the war is over, they bear the greater part of the burden of taxation. Therefore, I believe that an old age Pensions Act would only be evidence of our gratitude. I believe that it would help materially in creating a better understanding between capital and labour; it would be a public acknowledgment by the Government of this country that it wants justice for all classes, and it would perhaps abolish forever this unfortunate conflict between the capitalist and the labouring class. In proof of the soundness of our contentions, I have received, since I inscribed this resolution on the Order Paper, a number of letters and resolutions of labour unions in support of my views. They all wish me the greatest possible success in regard to this old age scheme. Amongst others, I might mention the following, from Mr. Beaule, president of the National Catholic Unions; from Mr. Tom Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada; from the secretary of the Liberal Labour Union of the city of Hull; from Mr. Achi'lle Morin, vice-president of the National Catholic Unions. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, this question is not a new one. An act for old age pensions was passed by the Imperial Parliament in 1908, and in 1911 the present Prime Minister, the Right Hon.

Lloyd George, brought down in the British House of Commons a bill under a different form, known as "The People's Insurance." In presenting this bill, he gave the following explanation:	"Considering that the
people are willing to help in furthering the progress and welfare of this country, the State, on the other hand, should give ample proof of its willingness to foster the welfare of the labouring class.
For ever so long France has had pension laws for old age and the disabled; it is, however, since 1905 that pensions have come to the fore. As early as 1883, there existed in Germany, insurances to provide for the workman, but it is especially the act passed in 1889 and amended in 1899 which brought relief to old age and the disabled. There exists in Denmark, an old age pension law; in New Zealand, parliament adopted such legislation in 1908.
After having shown what has taken place in Europe, Mr. Speaker, are we not allowed to hope that soon, we also shall have a law enacted which will provide for old age. Moreover, this question has already been considered by our own statesmen and the Canadian Parliament. I see, in Hansard, that during the 1907 session, Mr. Pringle, then member for Stormont, moved the f olio wing resolution:	That in
the opinion of this House, the subject of improving the condition of the aged, deserving poor and of providing for those of them who are helpless and infirm, is worthy of and should receive the early and careful attention of the government and of Parliament."
This motion, after having been discussed, was withdrawn. However, Mr. Pringle returned to the attack during the session of 1908, and moved the following resolution: "That a select committee be appointed to inquire, into and consider a ischeme oh schemes by state aid or otherwise for making provision for the aged and deserving poor, with special regard in case of any proposals of which they may approve, to their cost and probable financial results, and that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, and to examine witnesses on oath and affirmation. This resolution was adopted but nothing further was done. During the session of 1912, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and the then member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), the same person who was defeated by the present Deputy Speaker (Mr. Gordon), had both placed on the Order paper of the House a motion which called for the naming of a select

Old Age Pensions
committee to inquire into and report on a scheme of life-annuity for old age in Canada. As you will notice, Mr. Speaker, it is already more than fifteen years ago since the Canadian Parliament first took up this important question of Old age pensions. I 'believe that public opinion is ripe and that the Government should not delay any further action on this question. A pension fund has been provided for all those brave warriors who went overseas to protect civilization against German militarism and who have returned to this country sick and disabled, and it is quite right. A pension fund has been provided for the Civil Service; banks and other financial concerns provide a pension for their employees; alone these brave toilers, this army of workmen who were the pioneers of our industrial life, have not a pension fund to sustain them in their old age. I maintain that it is the duty of the nation to act immediately. It seems to me that men who have given thirty or forty years of their best years to the development of the resources of our country have a right to claim a pension when they come to the age when they are no more able to provide for their own support.
I have heard as an objection to this scheme, Mr. Speaker, that it would discourage thrift and personal ambition; the workman would not be as provident, knowing in advance that the Government is going to grant him relief in his old age. Well I do not consider this as being a serious objection. If this law should lead to abuses, as some people believe it would, the European countries where it is now in force would abolish it; but, on the contrary, they improve on it every year. Then the Government ought to abolish the retirement fund of the Civil Service and the banks and corporations ought to discontinue the pension fund for their employees. My opinion is that the law would stimulate the energy of the working men who would feel that they are backed up by the state. Immigration would also greatly benefit by the scheme when it would be known that in Canada we look after our people when they have grown old and disabled.
I do not intend going into details, for instance as to the age at which the pension should start, or the means of raising that pension fund; this can very well be determined when the bill is presented. What I want now is simply the recognition of the principle by the House, so that the Government would realize that they cannot
delay any longer the passing of such legislation.
I have before me now the copy of a speech delivered by Sir Wilfrid Laurier at a large meeting, held in Montreal, on the 27th of September, 1916, at which you were present, Mr. Speaker. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that as soon as the war would be over -the great Canadian foresaw already the victory of the Allies-one of the greatest questions would be that of the establishment of old age pensions, and to this end, he said he had entrusted to some of his most prominent Liberal supporters the task of inquiring into the subject. At the great Liberal convention held in Ottawa, in August, 1919, a special resolution was moved and adopted to that effect.
I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to raise a political question out of this resolution; I am fully confident that hon. members of this House, whether they sit on your right or on your left, will consider it on its merit. But I hope I shall be permitted to say that it is an essentially Liberal idea and that it would be proper for the Liberal party to carry it out. We, on this side of the House, should consider that wish expressed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1916 and embodied in a resolution at the great convention of the Liberal party in 1919, as an order to be cheerfully complied with.
I know that we are in a rather serious financial position, that we have an enormous debt and that the Government is endeavouring by all possible means to balance their budget for which they have the unqualified approval of the people. But this question of old age pensions should not be delayed any longer. Moreover I do not believe I am committing an indiscretion when I say that knowing the feelings of the hon. Prime Minister as I do and owing to the fact that he has made a thorough study of the social and economic conditions of our country, he is agreeable to this resolution and he will find a means of placing it on our statutes which will be a credit to him and a great asset for this country.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. CHARLES G. POWER (Quebec South) moved:	.
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to amend the act to provide pensions to or in respect of members of the Canadian Naval and Military Air Forces, 1919, so as to provide that the pension of a widowed mother of a member of the forces who has died on
Old Age Pensions

active service shall not be reduced on account of her income; and further that pension shall be granted her of right whether or not there are other living children.
He said: This is a resolution which, in one form or another, has come before the House for the past four sessions. In 1918, under the terms of the Pension Act for members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, the widowed mother of a deceased soldier was entitled to a pension of so much per month; but in case she earned anything, by working at any occupation whatsoever, the amount which she earned during the month was deducted from her pension. This provision, I am happy to say, has now disappeared, and the widowed mother, generally speaking, does not have any deduction made from her pension on account of her earnings. Further improvement was made in her lot somewhat later, when it was decided that even if she owned her own residence no deduction would be made from her pension by way of an amount to be attributed to rent; and a still further improvement was made somewhat later when it was decreed that the fact that she had one or more living children who were in a position to earn money and look after her should not be used as an excuse on the part of the Board of Pension Commissioners to take away the small pension which was given to her. At the present time the widowed mother, provided she is in a dependent condition, is entitled to $48 per month. Should she, however, have any income whatsoever the amount of this income is deducted from the pension. Should she have an income of $25, or $35, or $40 per month she receives that much less pension-that is to say in case her income is $30 per month, her pension would be only $18 per month. The object of this resolution is to place the widowed mother on exactly the same basis as the widow of a soldier who fell in France-in other words to give her a pension irrespective of whether she has or has not any income. As the members of the House are doubtless aware-and as I ' am sure, you, Mr. Speaker, know-the widow of a soldier who was killed at the war receives a pension without it being necessary for her to show that she is in a dependent condition. The object of this resolution is to place the widowed mother in exactly the same situation. During the past few years, those who are interested in soldiers and their dependents have noticed that there are a large number of complaints continually coming in to the 
Board of Pension Commissioners, to members of Parliament, to clergymen and others, that the widowed mother is being almost constantly visited by representatives of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment who enter into this lady's home, ask her how she is getting along, take a survey of the furniture, and inquire as to what her means of support are. If the old lady-because in the majority of cases, as the House can easily conceive, the recipients of these pensions are fairly well up in years-is unfortunate enough to explain her financial position and to state that she is doing nicely and getting along very well, the chances are that within two or three weeks a letter arrives from the Board of Pension Commissioners saying " You are in receipt of such an income; therefore your pension will be diminished by so much." It is with the object of avoiding any such occurrences that I would ask the House to approve of this resolution.
I have a number of cases which have been cited to this House and which have been brought to the attention of the pension commissioners on a number of occasions, and I do not think it is necessary to recite them here. I base my claim on behalf of the widowed mothers on the ordinary natural law and natural right. It has been urged on behalf of the former government that the mothers were not entitled to support from their children in other provinces of Canada except the province of Quebec. In that province the son, or the children, in fact, must support their parents, and an action at law will lie against those who will not do so. In other provinces of Canada, I understand, there is no such legal sanction to what, to my mind, is a natural right and a claim based on natural law. If it does not exist in the other provinces, I am sorry for those provinces, and I am sorry their legislators did not see fit to inscribe on the statutes of those provinces a law which has existed since the beginning of the world, and a law which should exist on the statute book of every province and every country. It is a purely natural law, and it is a natural thing that the son should support his mother when his mother is not in a position to support herself and should, in all cases, look after the mother who bore him, to see that she lives in comfort, if it is possible for him to do so. I submit it became the duty of the government of this country, as soon as the support of the

Old Age Pensions
family fell in battle, to look after those whom he left behind. In such a case I think it is the duty of the state to step into the breach and take the place of that son, who, no doubt, if he had not answered the call on behalf of his country, would now be able to keep his mother in good circumstances. There is the further argument, that we have recognized in the Pension Act a class, which though it is entitled perhaps to some consideration on the part of the government and of the state, surely is not entitled to as much, consideration as the class of widowed mothers. Section 34, subsection 1, of the Pension Act says:
A parent or any person in the place of a parent with respect of a member of the forces who has died shall be entitled to a pension when such member of the forces left no child, widow, or divorced wife who is entitled to a *pension, or a woman awarded a pension under subsection three of section thirty-three of this act, and when such parent or person is in a dependent condition and was, at the time of the death of such member of the forces, wholly or to a substantial extent, maintained by him.
Let us see what that means. The widowed mother of a soldier is entitled to a pension when the soldier has left no children- there is no objection to that,-or has left no widow, no divorced wife under certain conditions, or no woman awarded a pension under subsection 3 of section 33 of this act. Let us see who the woman referred to under subsection 3 of section 33 of this act is. That subsection says:
A woman who, although not married to the member of the forces, was living with him in Canada at the time he became a member of the forces and for a reasonable time previously thereto, and who at such time was publicly represented by him as his wife may, in the case of his death and in the discretion of the commission, be awarded a pension equivalent to the pension she would have received had she been his legal widow. The Commission may also award a pension if in its opinion an injustice would be done by not recognizing a woman as the wife of a member of the forces, although there is no evidence that she had been publicly represented by him as his wife.
Here is a case. The widowed mother whose son was killed at the front may obtain a pension, provided the man's mistress is not alive. If the mistress is living she has a prior claim to a pension from the state to that of the mother who bore him. It is not for me to criticise the legislation which has been placed on the statute book for what has been called the unmarried wife. I know that in a large number of compassionate cases something had to be done where there were children and where there was fraud on the part of the man who was unfortunately killed. I recognize that,
83 i
and I do not ask to have this provision removed from the act, but I do ask that the widow be placed at least in the same position as the woman I have just mentioned.
I think it is only fair, and only plain justice, to give to the mother, who, after all, has probably suffered more than any other class of person in this war, an opportunity of obtaining a pension. Let us, at any rate, be fair enough to admit that if there is one class that did suffer, if there is one class from whom bitter tears were wrung during the war, it was the widowed mother. It is more likely the widowed mother had more to endure, spent more anxious nights and wept more tears than any other class in the community. We have given pensions to almost everyone else, but this particular class. We have in the past, I think, been sadly deficient in our duty. It should be the duty of the House to support this resolution and put an end to the anomaly which exists in our present legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not in the House when my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) brought to its attention the question referred to in his motion. Therefore, I have been unable to appreciate the argument which he has submitted. As my hon. friend stated in the last part of his remarks, the particular case of the widow who has been deserted or abandoned by her husband is pitiable in the extreme. Although I am not in a position to discuss the question on its merits at the present moment, I would not prolong the discussion and would very humbly suggest to my hon. friend that he consent to withdraw his motion and submit the matter to the special parliamentary cotmmittee which has been appointed for the purpose of studying these questions, particularly, those relating to pensions and re-establishment. The committee would hear the representations which have been submitted by my hon. friend and could then offer a recommendation to the House when the time comes to prepare a report. I hope my hon. friend will find it agreeable to him to comply with this request. If, however, he desires to secure the opinion of the House on this question, I have, of course, no serious objection; but, as I said a minute ago, I think it is advisable that the committee should be advised of this matter, study it thoroughly, examine it in all its different phases and aspects with the idea of making a recommendation on the subject.
Old Age Pensions

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence): Mr. Speaker, this question of pensions is, day by day, becoming a matter of education; that is, we are receiving, as the days go by, more information as to the condition and the situation. Since the war and since the passage of the act, conditions have arisen that probably were not contemplated when that act was being passed, and I think we ought to have an open mind to deal with all these matters in the light of the new information we have. The hon. member for Quebece South (Mr. Power) spoke of instances in his experience where injustice had been done, unwittingly, of course, under the pension scheme provided for by the Pension Act as formerly drawn, to widowed mothers on account of their having some income from some other source. I must not criticise the Pension Act, of course, because one's hind-sight is wonderful; but, in the town in which I live, I came across two or three instances where the widowed mother was plainly entitled to a certain pension, but, as she had from a house a rental that did not begin to keep her and two or three other small items of income, she was deprived of a pension which, to my mind, she really ought to have received, as her two sons, one of whom was killed, performed magnificent services overseas. Under the peculiar working of the act she did not receive her pension, but that matter has been remedied.
In justice to my province, I might call attention to the fact that, in Ontario, we have an act such as the one my hon. friend mentioned, whereby children are compelled to support their parents. My hon. friend has given the House good reasons why this act should prevail throughout the Dominion of Canada; and if it were within the province of this House to make this a federal act, I would say: "Do so," because I firmly believe that there is nothing so lamentable in the world as to see parents moping about, uncared for, living, perhaps, in penury, depending on the charity of friends, while their children live in fairly comfortable circumstances and some far beyond comfortable circumstances. If a child has no regard for his or her parent, that is a time when the law ought to step in and compel him or her to perform that duty. I feel confident that, during the last two or three years, we placed such an act as that on the statute books of Ontario.
I am heartily in sympathy with the main point brought up by my hon friend in his

resolution. As the House has undertaken to cure the defects which applied to the widowed mother as regards the war land forces, the same action cannot be wrong if applied to the naval and air forces.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is away, I am not in a position to know how much this involves; but I am heartily in accord with the principle of the resolution as proposed by my hon. friend, and I should like to see some way by which it could be placed in a statute of this Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, possibly my hon. friend (Mr. Power), in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), would not press this particular motion to a division. I think it would involve some consideration as to the extent of the financial liability that is likely to be incurred, and the House should have knowledge on that point. In the meantime the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. Beland) has suggested that the committee might consider the matter. My hon. friend will know what to say as regards that; but I would like to ask him to consider the advisability of allowing his motion to stand, at any rate, until the Minister of Finance shall have an opportunity of speaking on it.
Hon. Sir HENRY L. DRAYTON (West York) : Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that what we ought to do at the present time is quite clear, perhaps, in some way, the motion of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) goes a little further than he intended it to go. There is no doubt as to the intent of the act, and that is to recognize the mother as she ought to be recognized, but, at the same time, treating the matter, as many other matters of pension are treated, namely, as a matter of application having regard to her necessity. If, in other words, she were a wealthy woman, I do not think my hon. friend believes that she should get a pension. I think his attitude is that the money should be left for other widows, widowed mothers and soldiers who are badly in need of it and that, as was the attitude of the late government, the need of the beneficiary of the pension was something that should be very much considered, and that the mere sacrifice itself was not sufficient, because it is impossible for Parliament to do justice to the sacrifice. It seems to me that the proper thing would be, not to have the motion withdrawn, as has been suggested, but to have it referred to the Standing Committee on Pensions where proper evi-

Old Age Pensions
dence can be taken and the matter properly considered and not lost sight of. I would suggest to the hon. member for Quebec South that the motion, instead of being withdrawn, should be referred to that committee.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Pensions Committee, I should like to say a word of assurance to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who moved the resolution. This point has been and is at the present time under discussion in that committee, and I can say that it is being discussed from a sympathetic standpoint. I think the ground we have taken in the discussion so far as it has gone, is that, as regards the point of having that pension cut down by the amount of income which the widowed mother received from other sources, every dependent, whether a widow or a widowed mother is entitled to a comfortable livelihood. We are trying now to amend the act so that that comfortable livelihood will be secured; but, as my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) says, the money will be applied, as far as possible, where it is most necessary. There are many cases of widows as well as widowed mothers where a small income is received from their own labours, where, in spite of lack of strength, they take in washing, or do small jobs around the place, or go out sewing, or take up different classes of labour for which they are not fitted, in order to augment the pension so as to make it sufficient to enable them to live in decent comfort. In those cases, the opinion of the committee is-perhaps I had better not say-

In those cases, legislation has already been introduced and passed to the effect that widows and widowed mothers do not lose any of their pension owing to their earnings, so that the committee was probably discussing something that was passed two or three yeas ago.

I was going to say that we included in that small incomes from other sources which were not sufficient in themselves to keep the widowed mother in decent circumstances. Our aim is to bring in a recommendation as soon as possible that will amend the act to cover these cases and provide as far as possible for the decent, comfortable maintenance of those women who have given their sons to the service of the country. We believe that the foundation principle is this, that the country owes them this as
the least it can possibly do for them; and that is what we are trying to do. I am not speaking against the motion; I am in favour of it. But I simply wish to reassure the hon. member that if the matter is referred to us it will be treated from a sympathetic point of view.

While possibly it is not strictly relevant to the subject before the House, nevertheless I think that the matter to which I wish to call attention now is apropos of the motion that has been proposed by my hon. friend. I wish to refer to a case that occurred in the constituency I have the honour to represent. Pour or five weeks ago a woman, whose son was killed at the front and who was receiving separation allowance and assigned pay, found herself in need of a pension. At the time her son was killed she was in receipt of separation allowance and assigned pay. She had a son-in-law who was assisting her and by means of that assistance, and other small aid and with what she had saved from her separation allowance and assigned pay, she was able to make out. But about six months ago she found herself absolutely without means, and she was faced with the alternative of securing a pension or going to the poorhouse. She appealed to me and I took up tne matter; but I am sorry to say that the department at Ottawa ruled against her. This woman's son met his death overseas; yet it was held that she was not entitled to a pension because three years had elapsed between the young man's death and the date of application for the pension. If that is the system that obtains in the matter of granting pensions in this country, then the sooner our people are informed to that effect, and the sooner we have done with this idle pretence about providing for the relatives of returned men, the better it will be for us all in Canada. I wrote to the minister and I think that probably I was very plain in the observations I made. I received very little satisfaction.
It is all very well for people to say that they have sympathy with the relatives of the men who were killed overseas. But sympathy will not support people of old age who have given their sons to the country's service. Sympathy and fine words will not keep them from going to the poorhouse, and the sooner we put away such maudlin pity and get down to the realities of life, the sooner we administer

Old Age Pensions
pension affairs on a basis of what is fair and equitable, the better it will be for all concerned. A few minutes ago the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Graham) was telling the House that he would like to see a federal act, if it-were within the competence of this Parliament to pass such, that would compel sons and daughters to protect and support their parents. I believe that there is at the present time a law similar to this, if not on all fours with it, in the province of Quebec. My hon. friend should remember that that province sets this Dominion a lesson in her urbanity and filial affection. Indeed, the people of Quebec are princes of the principles of urbanity, and the fapt that an English-speaking minister rises in this Parliament and says that he would like to see enacted in this country such a law as he has described, is not going to better things. Quebec has been very much abused, and coming, as I do, from the province of Nova Scotia, I must say that every true Canadian is thankful for the fact that there is such a province as Quebec where filial affection reigns supreme and urbanity prevails everywhere. I advise the Minister of Militia to go to his own province of Ontario and ask them to put this sort of thing into effect, rather than to ask the House of Commons to do it.

Mr. HANCE J. LOGAN (Cumberland) : Mr. Speaker, the resolution of my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) certainly commends itself to hon. members, particularly to those Who have had any experience of pension matters. Therefore I am not going to take up the time of the House, except to express my concurrence in the resolution and to suggest that its subject matter be referred to the committee
[Mr. Martell.l
which is now inquiring into pension grievances, as proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman).
We could multiply many times the grievances of fathers and widowed mothers in reference to refusals of pensions on the ground of the parents still having some earning power, but to do so would be only to repeat what has been already said this afternoon, and what is known to everyone who has had anything to do with pension matters.
I remember one case in particular of a mother whose four grown up boys volunteered for service when war broke out and went overseas. Her husband was subsequently injured in the spine in a mining accident and became an invalid. Three of the soldier boys were killed in action, and the survivor is still suffering physical injury due to war service. The invalid father died after lingering a few years, and the widowed mother is now compelled to maintain her other children, all quite young, and to do so she has to undertake work of the most menial character. She is a dear little woman, is an active worker in the Salvation Army, and has all the attributes of a good mother. This widowed mother of three sons who "lie in Flanders' fields" has now to maintain her family by cleaning the men's waiting-room in a railway station the floors of which are generally in a nasty condition. It is not creditable to Canada that this brave mother should be forced to do this disagreeable, menial work to maintain her family. She was granted a pension of $48 a month, but not long ago the Pension Board, on the ground, I believe, that this little mother was earning something, reduced the pension to $40-and to earn that " something " she has to go down on her knees and wipe the filth from waiting-room floors. That condition of affairs is a disgrace to this country and should never be allowed, and I hope that when this and like cases are reported to the committee they will make such strong representations that there will be no occasion for these mothers being any longer subjected to these indignities in order to discharge a duty to their dependents that should be discharged by the state.
I know of another case where a boy was forced to leave school at 14 years of age to maintain his mother. He volunteered when only eighteen or nineteen, went overseas, and was subsequently killed in action. His mother is now forced to maintain two little children by getting up at seven o'clock in

the morning and working for nine hours in a casket factory sewing shrouds on coffins. The Pension Board refused one cent of a pension either to her or her crippled husband, stating in their letter to the husband, dated March third last:
Under the provisions of the Canadian Pension Act pension may be awarded to the parent of a deceased soldier when such parent is in a dependent condition and is incapacitated though mental or physical infirmity from providing for his or her maintenance.
The Board of Pension Commissioners has decided that as you are not totally disabled but able to accept certain kinds of employment when available-
1 may say that this man is without some fingers of one hand and naturally is not able to secure employment when it is very difficult even for a man with both hands to get work.
-and as your wife and son are both earning, it is not possible to award you pension under the act.
I have already referred to what the wife is doing. The boy who is left, and who has now reached the age of fifteen years, has had to leave school in order to earn the paltry sum of $5 a week to help keep his mother and father from starving to death. His mother works in the casket factory, and the board have refused to pay her any pension although the boy was the means of her maintenance before he went overseas. These are cases, it seems to me, which will bring into disrepute the pension scheme of this country. Of course, we all realize how dangerous it is, from the financial standpoint, to open the door perhaps too wide. There are cases brought before the Pension Board which are not deserving, and no doubt somewhere the endeavour will be made "to put one over" the board, to use a common expression. But, Mr. Speaker, there are also cases such as the two I have mentioned, which show the necessity for an amendment to the act or for giving more discretion to the Pension Board of this great country.
I am not going to take up time further, believing that this matter will be thoroughly investigated by a committee, and that there will not be in the future such instances as I have brought to the attention of the House this evening, of parents whose children have made the supreme sacrifice being refused a decent pension because, forsooth, they are able to scrub a floor or work in a factory.
I would suggest that the hon. member have this matter referred to the commit-
Old Age Pensions
tee, but if he does not do so, I shall vote for the resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
speechtext:
I unfortunately left the Chamber about half-past five this afternoon and did not hear the discussion, but in reading over the resolution again-I had read it before-I feel that it has practically my total sympathy. I have had a number of cases at different times where the widowed mother of a soldier who was killed overseas in some branch of the service was receiving what seemed to me to be a very unfair deal. Such a case as my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Logan) has mentioned is an example of that kind. While it is true we are paying out an immense sum of pensions in this country, and true also that somebody may attempt to impose upon the Pension Board, at the same time I believe it is the duty of this Parliament and of the people of this country to do everything in their power to see that the mothers, as well as the wives and children, of the men who served overseas get a fair deal. I had a case very recently, which I think I have mentioned just in passing on another occasion, where the mother of a boy who was killed overseas had a couple of small houses rented in Port Arthur-she was not in my constituency but wrote me regarding the matter-and she went to England while she was getting a small rent from these houses. Later they became vacant, but because her case had been investigated and it had been reported that she was receiving a small rent her pension was cut down, or cancelled altogether, if I remember rightly, and according to her letter, which was almost pitiful, she was then receiving no rent at all. There is a great danger, I think, in taking into account some income which a widowed mother may have, because the investigator may be a little careless in his investigation, or even if he is thoroughly sincere, circumstances may change after he has made his investigation.
I am wholly in sympathy with such a resolution as this. I also agree with the last speaker (Mr. Logan) in his suggestion that perhaps this is a proper subject for discussion before the committee that is now sitting; but if the resolution should go to a vote, my sympathies would be entirely with it, and I should be compelled to support the mover.
There is just one other point I would mention. Occasionally there may be cases where some mother who does not receive
Old Age Pensions

a pension may impose upon the Pension Board and so upon the people of this country, but I believe the mothers of that type will be small in number. At any rate, it will be far better for this country to make the mistake of being too generous than to err on the other side and be too parsimonious in a matter of this kind.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton) :
speechtext:
As a member of last year's Pensions Committee I should like to say a word on this resolution. In the first place, it has my hearty sympathy and support. Although the act was amended last year to penalize the widowed mother more than she had ever been penalized before, it was done simply on the majority vote of last year's committee. As one of the committee, I was very much opposed to the amendment last year, which was to this effect: The original act provided that a widowed mother who had sons living at home with her would be supposed to be receiving $10 a month from each. The amendment last year widened that to include girls as well as boys. I believe the word "children" was substituted for the word "boys". Further than that, the amendment left it to the discretion of the board to decide whether or not that $10 should be deducted from the pension. I believe the exact wording was "any of the children either living at home or abroad who are contributing or are supposed to be contributing to the widowed mother's maintenance". That was partially offset by another provision which was made last year. Up until last year the widowed mother's earnings were deducted from her pension, I think, in toto, but last year it was provided that she could earn up to $20 without any deduction being made, this $20 including what was supposed to be contributed by the children.
With regard to referring this matter to the Pensions Committee, I sincerely hope that the mover of this resolution will not do that, for this reason: I was a member of that committee last year and am again this. We had a difference of opinion over this question in the committee last year, and we had a difference of opinion over it the year before, and the act as it now stands was only approved by a very small majority of last year's committee. I think the House itself should decide this important question rather than shelve it on to a small committee. Therefore, I hope that the mover will not withdraw the resolution or have it referred to the committee. I 
think the House itself should settle the matter.

There seems to be a slight misconception with regard to the purport of the resolution due, I think, to a misprint on the Order Paper. The resolution as printed on the Order Paper reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to amend the act to provide pensions to or in respect of members of the Canadian Naval and Military Air Forces.
The resolution should read:
Canadian Naval, Military and Air Forces.
Some hon. members were under the impression that the widowed mothers of members of the Canadian military forces had already obtained certain benefits which members of the naval and air forces had not obtained. In order to correct this impression, may I state to the House that the widowed mothers of all ex-soldiers and sailors and airmen are all on exactly the same basis?
I forgot to state this afternoon that not only are the ordinary widowed mothers, that is to say, the widowed mothers of Canadian soldiers, affected adversely by this legislation, but certain widowed mothers of Canadian soldiers who do not reside in Canada are more severely affected than others.
For instance, take the widowed mother of a soldier who enlisted from the United States. Take the widowed mother of a soldier who enlisted in Canada and was killed, who now resides in Scotland or in England. She is not treated with the same generosity as the widowed mothers who reside in Canada. Certain legislation was	passed improving the lot of
the	Canadian widowed mother, but
it was expressly stipulated that these improvements wouild only affect her so long as she remained in Canada. If she were to return, possibly to her old home, in Scotland or in England, her pension would be reduced by so much. If she returned to the United States the same thing would occur. I submit that the loss to the mother who resides in Scotland or the United States, or anywhere else in the world, is the same as the loss to the mother who resides in Canada; and legislation such as is aimed at in this resolution would do a great deal to improve the circumstances of these people.
Now with reference to the request which has been made by the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, by the Prime Minister, and by the Minister of Militia, I have

Mothers' Pensions
no objection out of deference to them, to referring the matter to the Pensions Committee; but let me say this: For five sessions I have moved this resolution in the House. On every occasion when it was debated as a resolution it would meet with almost unanimous support. Member after member has risen from his seat and given examples of the manner in which widowed mothers were treated throughout the country. The resolution was always sent to the parliamentary committee with the best wishes of, and a strong recommendation from, the members of the House; yet invariably when the findings of the committee were brought down and put in the form of legislation we found that the committee had been unwilling to go further than grant a paltry five or ten dollars a month extra to the widowed mother. On every occasion when the report of the committee came before the House I have endeavoured to have this legislation amended in order to give greater opportunity for this class to obtain proper pensions, and on two occasions at least, and possibly on three, my amendment has been ruled out of order by the Speaker on the ground that I have no power to amend the resolution of the committee on matters pertaining to a money bill. So that though I agree with my hon. leader and his colleagues, and, out of deference to them, have no objection to referring the resolution to the committee, I have very little hope that it will be put into legislation unless the members of the committee who are now present make it their business to see that a hard, strong fight is put up in the committee and that the wishes of the House are for once carried out by them.
Am I to understand the motion is referred to the committee?

speakeroldname: Mr. C. G. POWER (Quebec South) moved:
maintopic: PENSIONS TO MOTHERS OF DECEASED SOLDIERS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient that the Board of Pension Commissioners be given discretionary power to award pensions to mothers of deceased soldiers in cases where such mothers have been deserted by or become separated from their husbands, such pensions to be paid at the same rate as those awarded to widowed mothers.
He said: There is very little to be said with reference to this resolution. It asks the House to go on record as approving of the principle of treating the mothers of deceased soldiers who have been deserted, or become separated from their husbands, on the same basis as widowed mothers, provided always they can show their case a deserving one. It is in order to give effect to the latter provision that the resolution proposes to grant certain discretionary power to the Pension Commission. I may say it has been the experience of most of those who have had to do with the Board of Pension Commissioners that the less discretion we allow them the better it will be for the pensioner; but the number of and variety of cases dealt with here under this resolution is so great, that I do not wish to tie down the commission by any hard and fast rules. It may be possible later on to amend the law so as to give greater justice to all concerned; but I fear that if discretion is not allowed to the commissioners, a certain number of undeserving cases may obtain pensions.
In order to illustrate the cases I would like to see covered by legislation, allow me to cite one instance which occurred in my own constituency. There is a certain family in Quebec the children of which I have known for a number of years. When war broke out there were three boys, ail of whom enlisted for service overseas. Two returned very badly wounded, so badly wounded as to be unable to earn a living. One is now, I understand, under the care of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and the other is drawing a full disability pension. The third boy was unfortunately killed at the front. After some time his mother, whom I had always known as a widow, obtained a pension. Subsequently she was able to

St. Lawrence Waterway
obtain a small position as a charwoman in the post office. This year, two years and a half after the pension was granted, a visitor came to see this lady, and after making inquiries as to her financial condition, etc., went away. Two weeks afterwards a letter arrived which stated that the pension was cut off owing to the fact that this lady was now earning a certain amount of money at her employment at the post office. The case was referred to me, and I wrote to the chairman of the Board of Pension Commissioners calling their attention to the legislation which provided that the pension of a widowed mother was not to be reduced on account of her earnings. The reply I received from the Board of Pension Commissioners was, that everything I said was quite right but that the lady was not a widow. On making further inquiries 1 found that she had been deserted in the year 1894 by her husband -who would to-day be eighty-eight years of age if he were alive-and she has never heard of him since.
She will not obtain her pension unless she proves that she is a widow. It is to remedy cases like that, where, taking advantage of pure technicality, the Board of Pension Commissioners decided to cut off the pension that I propose to give them power to treat a woman in a case such as I have mentioned on the same basis as a widowed mother. It is not necessary to explain to the House that it would be a very costly proceeding for this old lady to employ detectives to find out where her husband was, and to advertise in the newspapers for him.
I need not say to the House that, under the law, at any rate of the province of Quebec, with regard to civil rights and with regard to property, after five years' absence a man can be declared an absentee; nor need I explain that in criminal matters-and this applies to the whole of Canada-a person can plead against the charge of bigamy that he or she has not heard from the other party for seven years. So that, when we have such provisions in our statutes already with reference to these matters, surely there should be a similar provision with reference to pensions. I submit it is absolutely unjust and unfair to ask a lady, in a case such as I have mentioned, to go to the expense of proving that she is a widow. I have been informed by the Board of Pension Commissioners that a large number of such cases exist throughout Canada, and that it would be a good thing if legislation were introduced to cover them. I think the Minister of Sol-

diers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. Beland) agrees with me that such cases should be looked after. I know a number of cases where, perhaps, there might be attempts at fraud, and it is for that reason that, at the present time, I propose to give a certain amount of discretion to the Board of Pension Commissioners. I think this resolution should, at least, on the face of it carry, and that it would not be necessary to refer it to any committee whatever. The case is absolutely plain and I look for an expression of approval on the part of the House.

House resumed, from April 26, consideration of the following proposed motion of Mr. Church:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government of Canada should give early and favourable consideration to the report of the International Joint Commission on the St. Lawrence River Waterway, and request the Government of the United States to join with Canada in making an international agreement for carrying out the work so recommended.

When the House adjourned on the day that this question was previously under consideration I had not had an opportunity to say the few words that I had in my mind on the subject. I commend, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) for bringing this question before the House. It is a subject of very great importance to the Dominion of Canada, and one which, I think, it is quite necessary to discuss more thoroughly than it can be discussed this session before we can bring the House and the country to realize their responsibility for carrying out this great project. For that reason I entirely disagree

St. Lawrence Waterway
with the hon. member from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) who indicated that it was a loss of time for the House to discuss a motion of this kind. It is only by discussing a project like this that the House can be brought to understand what it really means and that the country can be educated as to the necessity of so great a work.
My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle seems to think the object of this scheme is to increase the size of the city of Toronto. He may have got that idea from the fact that a representative of the city of Toronto brought it forward, but I think, if he will give it a little closer examination, he will discover that it is really to serve those parts of the country that are not congested in the form of great cities. To my mind this is a well balanced project that will be of benefit to every province of Canada, and it is one that has the approval of the International Joint Commission, and all members of the House have the report of that commission, I believe. It not only has their approval on the basis of an exhaustive examination of all the phases of the work, but it has the support of the President of the United States.
One of my hon. friends, I think the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) rather argued that that was an objection to it, that a partnership between the Dominion of Canada and the United States in a project of this kind was not desirable. I entirely disagree with that idea, because I think that a partnership that might be entered into by these two great countries to carry out this work is something that is desirable, and brings the project easily within the possibilities of the next few years. I am not at all alarmed, Sir, about entering into a partnership of this kind with the United States. I think these closer relationships in the development of both countries by a great project such as we are discussing is one of the things that bind us closer together, without bringing us under the same flag or under the same political system, and is calculated to continue for another century that hundred years of peace we have had between the two countries. I think, Sir, that the amity that has existed between the United States and Canada is due very largely to the maintenance of commercial and financial relations, and it is a happy thing to find the Dominion of Canada and United States co-operating with the International Joint Commission to carry through a work which is calculated to be of tremendous service,
in, my judgment, to every province in confederation.
This country has been endowed by Providence w^th the most wonderful system of inland waterways that can be found in any part of the world and while we have, in the past, done a good deal to improve those waterways, we are now face to face with a greater development than has ever before been conceived, and one which, I think, a close examination will show to be well within our financial resources and calculated to produce such results as would warrant the two countries in going on with the work. If we should sit down and refuse to develop the possibilities that are within our reach, we would surely be charged by later generations with lack of vision and courage. In the history of this country, there have been times when the amount of money involved would have been staggering; but, during the last ten or twelve years, we have got into the habit of speaking in terms of millions and sometimes of billions; and $100,000,000 or $250,000,000 is not to-day nearly so staggering a sum as it was a few years ago.
The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) drew attention the other day to the remarkable economy of using water instead of railway transportation. I do not think I need emphasize that further than to point out that, having such possibilities for water transportation, we ought to show some courage in developing them, because the saving in cost of transportation is going to be so enormous and because, with a recurring period of prosperity, the railway systems of this country and of this continent will be overtaxed as they were a few years ago. Canada has more miles of railway per thousand of population than, perhaps, is entirely necessary for the trade of the country. At the same time, if we can reduce the cost of transportation, especially to and from the great West, we are going to save the farmers of the West a tremendous amount of money, and we are going to make it possible for them to puchase goods manufactured in the East, and thus make our trade run east and west under the best and most economical conditions.
About two years ago, what is called car shortage occurred in Canada; men could not get cars to carry their goods. That was due to the remarkable prosperity that we enjoyed at that time. That condition is coming back, and it will not be many years, two or three, perhaps, before we shall be again
St. Lawrence Waterway

faced with the same conditions that existed two or three years ago, when there * was not a sufficient number of cars to handle the trade of the country. We cannot, of course, construct this waterway in time to meet that condition; but as we are certain to be faced with that in recurring periods in the future, we ought now to begin considering at what time we shall undertake this work in order to increase the transportaion facilities.
I said I thought this project was of great advantage to every province in the Dominion. What will be the effect of it upon the maritime provinces? I believe it would enable the miners of Nova Scotia to sell their coal in the greater part of Ontario. With a deep draught in the canal, with large boats carrying, perhaps, 10,000 tons, Nova Scotia coal could be sold as far west as Hamilton and the Niagara peninsula; it might go as far north as North Bay or further. If we could produce a condition of affairs by which coal from Nova Scotia could be sold throughout Ontario, that would be one of the greatest boons that could be given to that province. What is true of coal is true of steel, which is manufactured in Nova Scotia in large quantities. Steel is a kind of freight that requires cheap transportation, and vessels could be loaded at the steel mills and the product of those mills carried as far west as the head of the Great Lakes. Surely that would be of advantage to Nova Scotia. What is true of Nova Scotia is, of course, true of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island if those provinces have anything to sell. Probably the potatoes of New Brunswick would still go into Maine; but there have been times when potatoes of New Brunswick would have been very welcome in Ontario, and potatoes require a low freight rate. It would be easy to market, in the great centres of population, all that the maritime provinces generally produce, if we had cheaper transportation, and the only way of getting cheaper transportation is by water instead of by rail. This plan proposes and provides for that.
I think this project would be of equal value to Quebec. I know some hon. gentlemen think that Quebec will be injuriously affected by the canalization of the St. Lawrence. They probably think that the head of ocean navigation would be extended from Montreal further west. That would be true as regards tramp steamers and other regular lines of freight vessels; but Montreal would continue to be the head
[Mi, Hoc-ken.1
of ocean navigation for passenger traffic, because it is not designed, at least not in my mind, that passenger ships should go further west than the city of Montreal. The benefit that would accrue to Quebec, as I see the proposition, would be to have the products of the factories and industrial establishments of that province carried from the place of manufacture to the head of the Great Lakes at one-fifth or, pernaps, one-tenth of the freight cost that is now imposed by the railways. Many different manufactured products of Quebec could be sold in the western provinces under very much better conditions, if the cost of freight were reduced so enormously as it certainly would be by having the goods carried by water instead of by rail. In addition to that, no part of the Dominion of Canada can prosper without the great city of Montreal and other manufacturing cities of the province of Quebec enjoying their share of that prosperity.
I do not think any province in Canada can be prosperous without all the other provinces having their share of that prosperity; what makes for the good of one, makes for the good of all. And in this particular this proposed project, which has the approval not only of the men who have studied it most exhaustively but also of the great Republic to the south of us, is one that ought to commend itself to the business men of Quebec who are conducting the great industrial establishments there, as well as to the financial interests of that province which are all more or less tied up, inevitably and inextricably, with the prosperity of the manufacturers and industrial enterprises down there.
I do not think that any place would profit more by the carrying out of this project than would the city of Montreal itself. It is the great financial centre of Canada, and in that fact alone it would draw to itself a very large share of the prosperity resulting from the completion of this undertaking. I sometimes compare those who are writing against this project in the press of Quebec to those workmen who resisted years ago, and those who still resist, the introduction of labour saving machinery. I take it that increased efficiency in any part of our industrial or transportation systems would work to the general advantage of the whole country, and in that way the province of Quebec stands to gain quite as much as, if not more than, the province of Ontario. Ontario, I think, would gain, but not nearly as much as the province of Quebec. Que-

bee has a longer distance to carry its manufactured goods than Ontario and has to pay higher freight rates. But if we bad a waterway with regular lines of ships leaving Montreal and going up the St. Lawrence to the head of the lakes, any advantage western Ontario now has in the way of freight rates as against the province of Quebec would be wiped out; for the difference in the freight rate on a ship between Montreal and the head of the lakes, and between Toronto and the head of the lakes, is the merest possible fraction. So that I emphasize my argument that the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec stand to gain more than the province of Ontario.
I should think that all hon. gentlemen to my left would be among the protagonists of the project. It has been estimated that the cost of carrying grain from the West would be reduced by between five and ten cents a bushel. Let us put it at seven cents, and my hon. friends can figure out from that what a saving there would be in carrying the grain of the three western provinces by waterway instead of by rail.
On my hon. friend's calculation, how many million bushels of grain would it require to save the interest on the amount that would be spent on the undertaking?

I shall come to that question later. If we could reduce the cost of carrying grain to somewhere about 7 cents a bushel, and if we could proportionately reduce the cost of carrying manufactured goods to the West, the people of the prairie provinces would gain both ways. They would buy what they required from the East at lower prices, while they would sell to the East and to the markets overseas at a higher rate. So that it is my conviction that, if we except the province of British Columbia, every part of Canada stands to gain enormously by the construction of this work.
I am not going into the details of this matter, because they are to be found in this book to which reference has been made; and my hon. friend from North Toronto gave a great many details the other day. I am rather trying to deal with the subject in a general way. My hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) wants to know how much it would cost. Well, Sir, I am going to argue that it would not cost anything; I contend that the building of the canal would not cost the Dominion a cent. I have no doubt
that that assertion strikes my hon. friend from Lisgar as rather a startling one. But the basis of my argument is that in building the deep water canal in the St. Lawrence there would at the same time be developed for use in the Dominion of Canada-particularly in Ontario and Quebec- two million horse-power of electrical energy; and there would also be developed two million horse-power of energy for the United States. I venture to say that that four million horse-power of energy could be sold for enough to pay all overhead costs of the work both from the electrical and from the navigation point of view. If you take four million horse-power at $20 or $25 per horse-power, you have $100,000,000 a year, which, besides paying overhead costs, would probably pay all the costs of distributing the electrical energy and administering the navigation of the canal.
Would there be a demand for that horse power?

Not immediately, but if this work were started it is conceivable that it would take two or three years, or perhaps longer, to complete it, and during that time a good deal could be done to prepare the market for the energy that would be developed. But I would point out in this connection the fact that in the United States they are finding it not only desirable but profitable to electrify their railways, and a market would be found for a great deal of the power that would be developed as a result of this undertaking, in the electrifying of the railways of eastern Ontario and perhaps the western part of Quebec. At all events, it would not be a difficult or costly thing for the National railways to make preparations to operate all the line from Montreal to the Niagara frontier by electrical energy. And the time is coming when that system of transportation will be much more widely employed than it is to-day. There are a great many hundred miles of railway in the United States that are operated by electricity, which is by all odds the best motive power that a railway can have. In the first place, it saves about 10 per cent-I think it is estimated at 12 per cent-of the total weight that a locomotive has to haul. In water and fuel the steam locomotive has to haul 12 per cent of the weight of the train, and this could be eliminated by the use of electrical energy. In the next place, electricity is much more efficient in cold

weather, such as we have in this country occasionally. The electrical locomotive never freezes up, so that it is more dependable the colder the weather becomes; and, as an hon. member suggests, it absolutely removes the fire risk wherever it is employed. I think it will be found, before ten years have passed, that electricity will be recognized throughout this continent as the ideal motive power for all railways, and there, is going on in the United States at the present time a discussion as to whether they should not construct great central power plants to develop electrical power by coal at the pitmouth, transmitting that power to operate the railways two or three hundred miles away.
I am quite satisfied, Sir, from my amateur study of the railway problem of this continent that that is a development of the near future, and I make this digression in order to answer my hon. friend who asked me if there would be a demand for this power. I can tell him, as my hon. friend from North Toronto pointed out the other day, that where electrical energy is developed in large quantities there industrial activity is intensified, and what were formerly little villages or small towns soon develop into great industrial communities. Take the city of Welland alone, where there is an abundance of electrical power, and we find an outstanding example in our part of the province, of the growth of a small place into a considerable city. In the whole of western Ontario you will find few industries that are not operating with electrical power. In a word, electrical power is one of the principal factors that make western Ontario such a prosperous part of the Dominion. Electrical power has three great advantages over steam power-it is cheaper, it is cleaner, and it is more efficient. I could give you facts out of mv own experience, Sir, if that were necessary, but I do not think I need do so to bring myself within the judgment of hon. members. I have no fear that within a reasonably short period of time after this power were developed there would be a sufficient market to take up every horsepower of energy generated.
My hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) asked me about the financing of this project. There is a plan, Mr. Speaker, that I have discussed with one of the men who have been prominent in advocating this movement in the United States, and it commends itself to my judgment at least; whether it will satisfy the House or not is

another question. The plan is that this Government and the government of the United States might constitute a commission, for service and not for profit, with power to issue bonds to be guaranteed by both governments. I am afraid there are some persons in this country who do not like that expression; they would like to develop this great power on the St. Lawrence if it could be done for private profit. I think that would be a mistake. I am of opinion that we have gone far enough to discover that there are some things that can be done successfully by the public for the public; in fact, we have demonstrated this so fully in our own province that I feel satisfied this undertaking could be worked cut in an equally satisfactory manner.
Let us suppose, Mr. Speaker, that an international commission such as I speak of were created to carry out the plans that have been or will be prepared at a cost, say, of $250,000,000 or $300,000,000. That commission would undertake to work upon a reasonable recompense for their services; but not a cent would go to pay dividends; there would be no stock to pour water into. The commission would have power to sell the bonds, and I do not think any hon. member would hesitate to believe that if an international commission were created they could sell twice over all the bonds necessary to carry out the project, those bonds to bear a reasonable rate of interest, for they would have at their back the security of the whole North American continent, and would rely upon the earning capacity both of the canal and of the power to be generated, but particularly of the latter. It is primarily a navigation project, designed to take advantage of the great endowment that Providence has given to us; but with it goes the possibility of developing an enormously valuable asset as a byproduct of the extension of our deep-water navigation system from the gulf of St. Lawrence to the head of the lakes.
I should like hon. members to consider this project, not from any narrow, provincial or sectional standpoint, but from every standpoint. I have no expectation that we are going to settle it to-day, nor at this session, nor perhaps next session, but I anticipate that some member, if not my hon. friend from North Toronto, (Mr. Church) then his colleague from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), will certainly bring this question before the House at some subsequent session. If in the meantime hon. members will examine and study its relation to every province and
