realize the benefits that will accrue to each province from the completion of the project, I am satisfied that in the course of another session or two-I hope next session-the House will see its way clear to take a decided step towards inaugurating this work and carrying it to completion.
If we were asked to-day to raise $150,000,000 or $250,000,000 to carry out a work of this magnitude, I think we would all hesitate to take action. That is what my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) put to us the other day as an alternative. He said: If we are going to create a new navigation system, let us develop the Ottawa river practically from Montreal to lake Nipissing. Well, if we did that, we would have to go down in our own pockets to raise the necessary funds. We could not get a joint international commission appointed for such a purpose, we could not get assistance in financing from any other quarter. That consideration alone would seem to me to put that alternative out of the question at the present time. All the horsepower that could be developed from the Ottawa river, according to the figures of my hon. friend, is a million and a half. And that would be developed where? Not where it is needed, not where there is a market for it, but hundreds of miles away, with the result that much of that power would be lost in transmission. Besides, you cannot develop industrial communities of any size along the Ottawa river from this city up to lake Nipissing; that is absurd. Therefore any such electrical development would not amount to anything; but the development of electrical energy along the front of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec is something entirely different. There you already have a market, and there are the possibilities of a much more extended market. Further, by the use of this power that market would be constantly increasing and new industries would be established all the time, resulting in these two provinces becoming the great manufacturing centres of the Dominion-they are now, in fact, but they would then be much more so-and they would bring within reach of our country the possibility of developing foreign markets for our goods, because with cheap power we ought to be able to get lower costs of production, and with cheap transportation a vessel could load at any place in lake Ontario, lake Huron or lake Superior, as well as in the gulf or on the St. Lawrence river, and carry our manufactured goods to any part of the world.
Surely that is an alluring prospect that we ought to regard with keen sympathy
and deep interest. I submit, Sir, that there is no undertaking facing the people of Canada to-day that is so promising of results, so promising of increasing our national prosperity and of such extraordinary value to us as the carrying out of this great work; and the adoption of this resolution submitted by my hon. friend from North Toronto would be the first step to this desirable consummation.

I
cannot allow this resolution to be finally disposed of without taking some part in the discussion. Knowing the circumstances surrounding this matter and the conditions in connection with electrical power development fairly well, I feel that there is no question of greater importance or of greater interest that could come before this Parliament at this or any other session than the resolution which is now under discussion.
I notice that my hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) in his speech on Wednesday last said:
As to improving the navigability of the St. Lawrence, there is a lurking suspicion that this is only the ostensible purpose, and that the real purpose of the promoters is to promote water-power-
I wish to disabuse my hon. friend's mind of that idea at once. He is quite mistaken in supposing that the ostensible purpose of the promoters is to promote water-power, and when he speaks of promoting water-power, I apprehend that he means promoting water-power in so far as the development of electrical energy by water-power is concerned.
This proposition took its rise, in the first place, in the middle western states. Some eighteen or twenty of these important states feeling that it was necessary for the wellbeing of that great country that there should be better water transportation facilities between the Great Lakes and the ocean, formed an organization called the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Tidewater Association for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the United States government the necessity of making the St. Lawrence river navigable from the Great Lakes to the ocean. That was practically the inauguration of this scheme, and the electrical power development only came into it when Canadians here interested in this matter took the question up themselves.
The American Tidewater Association had its formation twelve or fifteen years

ago, and spent enormous sums of money in propaganda and publicity through the United States. Some four or five years ago a number of enthusiastic gentlemen in Canada felt that there should be a greater interest taken in this matter not only by our Canadian citizens, but by the Government of Canada, and they formed in the city of Windsor an association known as the Canadian Deep Waterway and Power Association, to act in conjunction with the United States association for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the two governments the benefits that would accrue from the undertaking and completion of this project, and through the Canadian association the great possibility of paying for the whole project by the development of electrical current. That is where the electrical element entered into the consideration of the matter.
A good deal has been said about the enormous expense, and I intend to-night to devote my time and what ability I have to dealing with that side of the matter. I notice my hon. friend from St. James in his speech the other day said:
I want to remind the House also of some of the very good reasons which have been advanced why the Government should be very cautious in this matter-
I agree with him that the Government should be cautious.
-should approach the whole question warily-
I quite agree that we should act warily.
-and should refrain at the present time from taking the least practical action.
Why refrain? We can act cautiously, we can act warily, but it would not be the part of courageous citizens of Canada for us to refrain altogether from taking up this matter and endeavouring to deal with it as a business proposition in connection with an application to the United States government with a view to arriving at some practical understanding in regard to it. I think that we are quite capable, so far as the business end of it is concerned, of taking care of ourselves. We understand the matter as fully as they do, and I have no fear at all from that point of view.
Let us see in the first instance what the expense of this project will be. We have the engineers' estimates. It was stated by my hon. friend from St. James that possibly their estimate would not cover one-half the cost. Let me state that the engineers prepared their estimates last summer. They

were published in August, and the details of the expenditure were also published. Those details have been in the hands of engineers who have been opposed to this project from that hour until now, and the fact that they have not up to this minute pointed out one error in the calculations of the engineers is the best evidence to my mind that their estimates are correct.
What do the engineers say? They say that the cost of the project will be $252,723,200, and that this amount will be required to make the St. Lawrence navigable from the lakes to the ocean and create an electrical power development on the international section of the river by which there will be developed 1,464,000 electrical horsepower. Those figures $252,723,200 are rather staggering, and it is necssary that we should know where this is going to lead before we attempt such enormous expenditure, even in conjunction with the wealthy United States of America. What does it mean? I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Hocken) in his remarks as to the financial end of this proposition. I understood him to say that he favoured the appointment of a joint commission. If the Government should incorporate what might be called the Joint International Navigation and Power Company with authority to issue, say, fifty year debentures, those debentures to be guaranteed by the governments of the United States and Canada, I submit to hon. members of this House that those debentures so issued could be readily sold at four per cent interest. Assuming that to be the case, the annual interest at four per cent on the capital expenditure would be $10,108,928. The annual cost of operation and maintenance as outlined by the engineers amounts to $2,562,000. The sinking fund to pay off that capital expenditure in fifty years would amount to $3,300,000 a year, making a total expenditure of $15,970,928 a year. This is an enormous expenditure but what have you got for it? You have electrical power amounting to 1,464,000 horse-power and at $12 per horse-power on the switchboard that would amount to $17,568,000, or a surplus over the annual expenditure sufficient to wipe off the whole indebtedness, upkeep and maintenance of $1,597,072.
Now I appeal to my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Rinfret) if the Montreal Light Heat and Power Company sell current at the switchboard at their works in the St. Lawrence river at $12 a horsepower? That is an exceedingly cheap elec-

Now what does this report say in so far as expenditure is concerned.
In the first place let me point out what the report says in relation to the Welland canal, but first I want hon. gentlemen to remember this:	We are at the outset faced
with an expenditure of $80,000,000 for the construction of a new Welland ship canal. The Government of Canada is faced with that proposition. The estimates for the expense of that work were made in 1912, and the original estimate made at that time was for $50,000,000. The work would have been completed long before this, and well within that expenditure, had it not been for the cruel war which upset everyone's calculations and set the world back many years. Now with the increased cost, that expenditure is extended to about $80,000,000. The commissioners say this:
Another factor in the situation that should not be lost sight of is the peculiar relationship to the proposed improvement of the new Welland ship canal, a portion of which is now under construction. As pointed out in an earlier part of this report, the completion of the Welland ship canal and the adoption and completion of the St. Lawrence Improvement would remove the only barrier to the creation of a deep-water route from the head of the lakes to the sea. This would give at least 25-foot navigation from the sea up to the Detroit river, with a present minimum of about 20 feet above lake Erie. Although entirely outside the strict terms of the reference submitted to it by the two governments, the commission has been impressed by the fact that the new Welland ship canal
is such an integral part of the waterway, and is so inseparately interwoven with the project under immediate consideration, that it should properly be considered as a part of the whole scheme and the expense of its construction should be apportioned between the two governments upon the same basis as the works recommended for the upper St. Lawrence.
So that we have at the outset this International Joint Commission recommending that the Welland ship canal be taken into consideration as a part of the whole project, and that the cost of this construction be apportioned between the two countries on the same basis as the upper St. Lawrence. Then they say in their recommendation :
1.	The governments of the United States and Canada enter into an arrangement by way of treaty for a scheme of improvement of the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and lake Ontario.
2.	That the new Welland ship canal be embodied in said scheme and treated as a part thereof.
Now how is that to be apportioned? It is recommended:
That, except as set forth in recommendation (11), the cost of all "navigation works" be apportioned between the two countries on the basis of the benefits each will receive from the new waterway:	Provided, That during the
period ending five years after the completion of the works-and to be known as the Construction Period-the ratio fixing the amount chargeable to each country shall be determined upon certain known factors such as the developed resources and foreign and coastwise trade of each country within the territory economically tributary to the proposed waterway, and that that ratio shall be adjusted every five years thereafter and based upon the freight tonnage of each country actually using the waterway during the previous five year period.
Now will any hon. member say that if that proposition of the commissioners was carried out, the ratio of cost would be a fifty per cent ratio? Everyone knows that the United States will benefit eight or ten times more than Canada will for the next fifty years from the construction of this St. Lawrence waterway, and that is the basis of their calculation but, assuming the ratio is three to one, that we pay one-quarter of the expense and the United States government pay three-quarters- I am not committing myself to that ratio of expenditure; I think it would be too great so far as Canada is concerned, but let us assume as a basis of argument for submitting this question to the people that the ratio of expenditure would be as three to one, three to the United States and one to Canada-what does that mean at once? The Welland canal will cost $80,000,000. Instead of Canada paying $80,-

Now what will he the expense of the St. Lawrence waterways? Figuring on that basis-because that is the basis I submit we should figure it on, not a fifty-fifty ratio but something in the nature of the proposition submitted by the commissioners- the St. Lawrence river is divided in so far as this project is concerned, into five sections. The cost of operation and maintenance would be $1,671,000 according to the engineer's report; and the sinking fund to pay off that total amount in fifty years would amount to $1,300,000 or a total per annum of $7,098,154, which would be Canada's separate liability in connection with this project assuming that Canada was to pay one-fourth and the United States three-fourths of the total expense.
Now, what do we have? Canada's part of the electrical power development would be 732,000 horse-power which at $10 per horse-power would give $7,320,000. At $10 per horse-power it would pay Canada's whole liability in connection with that matter and leave about $300,000 per annum of a national profit. At $12 per horsepower the proceeds of the sale of the power would be $8,784,000, or a surplus over and above Canada's share of the expenditure of $1,500,000 a year. If those figures are accurate, if that is what it will produce, if the construction of this project, the development of the electrical current, the completion of the waterway, will work out in that way truly from the figures, surely it is a good financial proposition for Canada to enter into and we need not fear the

consequence. Those figures are accurate, so far as we have them up to the present time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the very next question which will be asked will be:	Can
that power be sold in the market? Can 732,000 electrical horse-power be sold either at $10 or $12 per horse-power readily and speedily? I submit, without any hesitation, that it can. In connection with the electrical power development and the disposal of electrical energy, there can be no market for that electrical energy until the electrical energy is produced. It does not create a market itself, in advance of production. The experience of the past has shown that. People will not prepare for taking electrical energy, or establish plants for using electrical energy until it is ready to be distributed to their plant and their operation. Let us see what happened in the case of Niagara Falls; because it seems to me that what has happened in the past is very likely to happen in the future, and that we can govern our future action by the experience of the past. Twenty years ago there was not one horse-power of electrical energy developed at Niagara Falls, or in the Niagara peninsula. At that time the Ontario Power Company first began to develop its power, and it was said publicly and privately that it would be practically impossible to transmit electrical current from Niagara Falls to Toronto with commercial success. From that day till now there has been developed in that Niagara district. Niagara Falls and DeCew Falls, and is being distributed, used and paid for, not throughout Ontario, but from Toronto west to the Detroit river, about

The commission has before it graphs Nos 3 and 5 showing the present use of power on both sides of the boundary within a radius of approximately 300 miles of the Long Sault rapids, and also the probable future demand. It appears from these graphs that at the present time (1921) the total primary power installation on the United States side of the 300-mile area is approximately 9,900,000 horse-power and on the Canadian side 1,900,000 horse-power. But, Sir, you may say that is conjecture. Let us get down somewhat to the actual. There was a resolution moved in this House some weeks ago in reference to electrifying our steam railways. My hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Hocken) referred to that question to some extent, but I wish to enlarge a little, because I have some figures as to the actual power which will be used. In the first place, in operating railroads with electrical energy they do not consume anything like the amount of power that is required in the case of operation by steam, because, by some system in connection with the operation, the electrical energy is returned to the line. When the electrical locomotive is standing still the current is not being used, when it is going down grade the current is not being used, but it is being returned to the line, whereas with the steam locomotive the fire is kept up and the steam is being generated continually, whether it is in motion or not. Let us, in the first place, consider whether the railroad can be economically operated by electrical energy. I have in my hand a little pamphlet which has been issued by the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad, and in this pamphlet I find the following:
From the outset the operation of electric locomotives has been a success, and he states
that they have practically eliminated the mountain grades. The large number of helper engines originally used to handle the passenger and freight trains over the mountain grades has been replaced by one or two electric locomotives, which alone are sufficient to handle the greatly increased traffic of the present year (1915). The movement of trains is so uniform and failures of electric locomotives so infrequent, that one set of train despatches takes the place of two sets employed under steam operation.
Electrification has made, it possible to increase the tonnage on maximum grades from 1,700 to 2,500 tons per train and this latter will be further increased to 3,000 tons shortly. This increased tonnage is now being handled at a speed of 15 mp.h. as compared with 8 m.p.h. by steam.	'
The winter of 1914-15 demonstrated in a practical manner that while the steam engine is at its lowest efficiency in cold weather, the electric locomotive, on the other hand, is at its maximum.
There were long periods, in the Rocky mountain district, when the thermometer registered 40 degrees below zero and it was impossible to-move the trains by steam locomotives. The electric locomotives, however, were always ready for service, and always able to work to the maximum.
In the practical operation of the transcontinental trains of the C.M. & St. P. over the Rocky mountain grades the train is brought to the summit at a speed of from 23 to 25 miles per hour. There is no difficulty in obtaining a speed of 60 m.p.h. on level grades, with 10 allsteel cars.
Experience has shown that the electric locomotive handles about 3J times as many ton-miles per month as the steam locomotives, and it also appears that the electric locomotives cut 30 per cent from the time necessary to do a given business, partly by running faster and partly by moving heavier trains.
This is conclusive proof that steam railways can be electrified and operated to advantage by electric current. There would, to my mind, be no better place on the North American continent to test out the working of electric railway operation than over the Canadian National lines between the city of Montreal and the city of Toronto. Between Montreal and Toronto there is used approximately 25,000 steam horsepower for road service and yard service.

that can he developed on the international section of the river.
It can very fairly be said that if there were no market in Canada for the one-half of the electrical power that can be developed on the international section of the St. Lawrence, it would be advantageous to us to sell it to the United States, temporarily at any rate, until we could secure a market for ourselves. But when, practically within a stone's throw of the great metropolitan city of Montreal, we can develop 2,636,000 horse power at a cost of very much less than $100 per horse power, how can any one stand up and fairly argue against this project being not only undertaken but carried to completion at a very early date? The power that we shall have is not for a day, nor for a year, nor for a hundred years. So long as the sun shall shine, so long as moisture rises from the earth, and rains descend from the clouds, so long as the eternal hills shall stand, so long will this mighty St. Lawrence roll that enormous wealth of power from the Great Lakes to the ocean. And shall we stand idly by and allow this wealth to go past us undeveloped and unused? My hon. friend from St. James said the other day:
If the flow of the St. Lawrence was as abundant and tumultuous as the faculty of speech of my hon. friend (Mr. Church), we might take chances with it, but in my view the St. Lawrence is too precious an asset to this country for us to lightly and without the strongest motives either attempt to alter its navigability, or enter into partnership with another country in regard to it, or place a mortgage on our property rights in it.
We are not asking any one to enter into partnership with any country, nor do we propose to alter the navigability of the river. It is navigable now going downstream, but it is not navigable upstream. It has a mighty current of power going from the Great Lakes to the ocean, power which will flow for all time and furnish the motive force to turn every wheel of commerce within the radius to which electrical energy can be transmitted; and if that mighty power is to be put to use, now is the time to do it. Now is the time for us in Canada, with all the enormous obligations we have to shoulder, with our great railway deficits, to put to use this, the greatest available power which this or any other country has. Enter into partnership with other countries? Let me assure my hon. friend that at this hour the United States government, under treaty rights with Great Britain, has
the free right to the navigation of the St. Lawrence, just as we have. We could not stop them without violating that treaty, and all that they are asking for now is that that river be made navigable, so that ocean going ships can go from tidewater to the head of the Great Lakes. We say that we in Canada could not possibly consider that enormous expenditure for one instant unless there were coupled with it a development which would pay the cost of that construction; and we point out to this House and to the country the advantages, not only possible but certain which would accrue from the electrical development, and we ask the House to join us in supporting the resolution.
Now, can we not go further? If this is a financially feasible proposition, is the navigable channel not in itself advantageous? Can we not with confidence appeal to our Progressive friends from the prairie provinces to assist in the completion of this project? Hon. gentlemen from that section say: "'We want the Hudson Bay railway built." Very well, I supported appropriations for the construction of that railway in the past, and I am prepared to sup port appropriations for the same purpose in the future. I believe the Hudson Bay railway to be a necessary part of the transportation system of the great Northwest. Will the people of the West not more speedily secure the construction of the Hudson Bay railway by increasing the national wealth of the country? And can you not increase the national wealth by constructing this St. Lawrence waterway? The people of the West say they want cheap freight rates and greater transportation facilities. Then let hon. gentlemen from that part of the country join with us in bringing about the completion of this project, which would reduce freight rates by at least ten cents a bushel on over 300,000,000 bushels of wheat which is to be moved from the great prairies to the city of Liverpool. My hon. friend (Mr. Hocken) figures upon a saving of seven cents a bushel. I say that undoubtedly ten cents a bushel could be saved on wheat shipped from the prairies to Liverpool if the grain were carried by water. It is well known that water transportation is by far the cheapest system of transportation there is. I urge hon. members to support the completion of this great undertaking. We cannot afford to stand idle any longer in this important matter. As was said of Britain's statesmen by one of her noblest poets, "Let us know the season when to take occasion

by the hand and make the bounds of progress broader yet." That is the idea we have in mind in endeavouring to carry through this proposition.
Let me put three points in a nutshell. In the first place, at the lowest calculation, we could save $60,000,000 in the construction of the Welland ship canal. Is that worth going after? In the next place, we could save $3,000,000 to $5,000,000 a year in the operation of the Canadian National Railway system. Is that worth considering? In the third place, there would be saved to the farmers of Canada 10 cents per bushel on over 300,000,000 bushels of wheat shipped from the Northwest to Liverpool. Is it worth while trying to secure that advantage? Place those three factors by themselves and then say to yourselves: Can we secure these three things without costing the taxpayers one dollar? If we can, it is our duty as citizens of Canada, true to our country and true to ourselves, to enter into this project wholeheartedly and carry it to completion at the earliest possible date.
We cannot, I say, afford to wait. I have no fear of any complications arising between Canada and the United States regarding a few acres of submerged land in the St. Lawrence river; that land is covered by water now, and it will be covered by water for all time to come. I have no fear of any serious questions arising between Canada and the United States regarding any agreements which we may enter into in respect to this matter. Peace has reigned between us for the last one hundred years, and I feel confident that peace will continue to reign for hundreds of years yet to come. We are all Anglo-Saxons talking the same language and holding the same religious convictions practically, and there can be no serious differences of opinion between these two great countries.
Let us enter into this undertaking energetically, let us carry it out intelligently and as economically as possible, and then this great Canadian ship of state will be headed down the channel of time to a sure harbour of unbounded prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, this question must be looked at in the broadest manner, for it is a continental question; it concerns the whole North American continent and not merely the United States or Canada. It is part of the policy of the development of the St. Lawrence river by the United States, and there should be the same policy in Canada for this development of our St. Lawrence
TMt. German.]
waterways. We have a splendid example in the achievement of the United States in building the Panama canal. That canal is a little slow in bringing its usefulness to the world in cheaper transportation, but it is doing so now. That canal cost billions of money to build, and it was completed in less than ten years. It was undertaken largely through the enterprise and foresight of the late President Roosevelt. Now President Harding has taken up this question, and he has been moved to do so by two main arguments put forward by the farmers of the United States for cheaper transportation. The Farmers' bloc at Washington is now so strong that at every point they are securing the majority support of Congress and of the President's cabinet, and only the other day the President himself made a deliverance in favour of the development of the St. Lawrence waters that committed him and his party to its support.
The farmers of the western states have found out, just as have our farmers in the western provinces, that railway rates are too high, principally due, perhaps, to bad management of their railways. Indeed, all the railroad organizations of the United States have come to the same conclusion, and they are now shaping up a policy for the rehabilitation of their properties, and through their chief speakers and organs they have declared that to lower freight rates and so increase traffic they must electrify their roads. There cannot be the cheap transportation we expect from our railways unless they are driven by electrical energy. There is an abundance of electrical energy along the St. Lawrence, coupled with other water-powers, to drive the trains on every railroad line in the northern portion of the states from Chicago to Philadelphia.
As my hon. friend (Mr. German) pointed out a few minutes ago, until quite recently electric energy could not be transmitted for more than fifty miles because of the excessive leakage of current; but the latest discoveries of science point to the feasibility in the near future of electrical energy being transmitted for five hundred or even a thousand miles without any appreciable leakage. The electrical art is developing very rapidly, and the employment of new methods render possible to-day what was out of the question a few years ago. Take the introduction of aluminum, for instance: only a few years ago it was regarded as a curiosity, but to-day it is being used for transmission wires, and in that way the

St. Lawrence Waterway
length of transmission is greatly extended. The first company to discover its possibilities was the Aluminum Company of the United States, and ten years ago they very nearly obtained control of valuable water power at Cornwall on the St. Lawrence. It was just by a mere chance that a few members in the railway committee at that time prevented that great water-power passing into the hands of United States citizens.
The pressing need of the railways of the United States to-day is electrical energy. I quoted some of their articles to that effect when I last spoke in this House. They are now trying to reorganize their railroads into ten regional divisions and electrify them. That electrification will cost a lot of money, but it will be spent in labour and equipment to the advantage of the country generally, and with electrification will come reduced freight rates.
Our farmers know that the supreme question to-day is cheap transportation. They know how high freight rates have been and still are by reason of the use of steam power and other circumstances, and they have reached the same conclusion as the President of the United States and the Farmers' Bloc, that electrification of the railways must come and will come almost immediately. The United States railways have their plans prepared for this electrification, and the president's move to develop energy on the St. Lawrence waterways has two objects in view-first, the improvement of the waterways for navigation and transportation purposes, and, secondly, the production of energy for the electrification of the railways of the United States.
Now, all the American railways to-day have placed themselves on record in favour of the substitution of electrical energy for steam. They have done so for several reasons, among others, because electrical energy is cheaper, because it is more reliable, and because the supply is unlimited, and they all know that scientific discoveries are proceeding at such a rapid rate that the transmission of electrical energy is already practical for long distances.
Let me tell you what took place in our own province of Ontario on the Niagara river. Sir Adam Beck has been much criticised for the expenditure involved in developing the Chippawa-Queenston generating plant. In one year from now that plant, owned by the municipalities of Ontario, will be developing 500,000 horsepower, and I believe within two years 1,000,000 horse-power, and will be driving every train in Ontario not only from the Detroit river to Montreal but even up to lake Nipissing. That may be merely a dream in the opinion of some people, but I do not think so1. Would anyone have dreamed twenty-four months ago of the present radio development? No one would have prophesized that such rapid progress would have been possible. No one can foretell its ultimate development, nor what it may mean in revolutionizing the whole world through the use of radio waves. The use of these radio waves is going to reorganize probably the whole world. The hope of scientists is that they are going to be able to transmit electrical energy even without the wiring. That is not a dream; it is almost at hand. So we do not need to go by visions; it is in sight now. In twelve months there will be a quarter of a million, and in two years half a million horse-power developed at that one plant. There may be a change even in the developing plants on the river bank there. The Chippawa plant would probably scrap some of the plants now developing near the river in not so advantageous a position. This project, then, is no impractical vision.
The statement is made in this House and in some of the papers that Montreal would object to this project because its supremacy in transportation would be threatened. The effect will be to make Montreal a greater city. How could Montreal people talk that way, living within a few miles of the home of La Salle, when they think of the dream he had of what the St. Lawrence would eventually become? He was the first man to go up the Niagara and build the first boat near the Falls and sail up to lake Superior. So as far as Montreal is concerned, this project will make it an even greater city. Most of the water-power is near that city, and this development will make it one of the greatest cities on the continent. No matter how much power is developed there, it will always find an immediate market. The American roads will be ready to buy it, for they have already made up their minds that they must electrify, and they must get power. The President of the United States has committed the government of that country to this development, and the farmers in the United States are behind him, just as our farmers here are beginning to see that the relief to transportation must come
St. Lawrence Waterway

from the competition of the waterways. The competition of the waterways in former days failed largely because of the opposition of the railways, but the new doctrine of to-day is that the railways are the complement of the waterways and the waterways the complement of the railways, and both working in competition will produce lower freight rates. They will be bound to produce lower freight rates, and the saving will be such that it will justify ten times over the commitment in connection with the construction of the waterways on the St. Lawrence as outlined in the commission's report.
I had intended when the railway question came up, which we may be discussing in the House this next week, to refer to these things, but the opportunity seemed to present itself to-night to speak on the line I have followed. Certainly I have not come to my conclusions in a short time simply by reading what has been said recently, for the whole tendency of investigation and of scientific discovery is in the direction of the development of waterpower and of the development of waterways for transportation. In this case it will work out both for the development of power and the improvement of transportation. That development of power will be for the benefit not only of the railways but of the cities. It will make the provinces here in the East better off, and the provinces in the West better off. To say that it might stop at this city or that, or that what is now in Montreal would go to Toronto, is not to appreciate the effects of this development. There need be no rivalry; there is room for all. All the cities will improve, and they ought all to join together in the proposition, as I believe they will eventually.
I want to tell my friends from the West that years ago there were men in this country, as there were in the United States, who not only saw these waterways being extended to lake Superior, to the so-called head of navigation, but that canalization could be carried on to Winnipeg and to the foot of the Rocky mountains. That has all been worked out, and it is quite a feasible proposition to canalize the waters of the St. Lawrence up to lake Superior and right through to the valley of the Assiniboine and the Saskatchewan, connecting them up with other water systems up there to provide a system of canals that would carry the freight of the West right down to the seaboard. Some 
might say, would not that injure our railways? I say, no; it would develop the West. Link up these waterways and there will be all the business our Canadian railways could ever want or ever handle. There is room for both; one improves the other; they are complementary, not in opposition. This development would carry improvement to other cities and provinces. As for Montreal, it has a great future before it. There are millions of horse-power right at her door. She has developed her horse-power in the past. All I would like to see is that hereafter the great development of this electrical energy shall be done by the state, and not by private owned companies. We are doing that in Ontario, and we have set an example to all the world in that one plant at Chippawa. It is a new river that has been made use of, and a most powerful one; on that river we see the greatest development of electrical energy yet known to the world, and within two years or a little more, it will be producing one million horse power with a revenue of $10,000,000, and it will not have cost $100,000,000 for its construction. That power will be the life blood of Ontario just as the development of the water-power on the St. Lawrence will be the life blood of Montreal and the province of Quebec.
There is no question of rivalry between cities or provinces, for the whole project works out to the benefit of all the cities and provinces, and not only for the benefit of Canada but of the United States as well. It is a great continental question. The United States is looking at the great problems of the day from the national point of view. I have been reading to-day, and I have read a good deal of late about it, the report of a special Senate committee in Washington in the way of improving the banking system of the United States. They have made a great deal of progress in their banking system. They have a scheme now before Congress for the creation of a great organization backed by the credit of the United States to develop some kind of national marketing of the wheat and cotton crop and all the products of the Mississippi valley so as to get the best prices, and in connection with that they are going to develop the water-powers and waterways so as to give cheap transportation. All of these questions are in the air now, and you will see them move very rapidly. You will see the people of the United States who built the Panama canal prepared to do their share in the development of the St.

St. Lawrence Waterway
Lawrence waterways, both for power and transportation.
The expense is comparatively a small one, after the experience of the United States with the Panama canal. I should not like to say how many millions it has cost, but it cost a very large sum of money, and the United States never felt it. The Panama canal is one of the things that has made the United States the commanding power it is in the world to-day. They have built the Panama canal and they propose now to assist us to develop the St. Lawrence waterway. They have set an example to the world in great legislation for improving transportation, for improving the condition of the farmers; in making these issues national issues, and making them national propositions instead of company propositions. I have nothing to say against the railway companies which have done so much both in Canada and the United States in the way of developing transportation. But in the United States they have not been very successful. The net result of their exploitation of the railways there is that eighty per cent of those railways would be bankrupt today if it were not for the assistance which the American government gave them in connection with the war. The same authority will have to find money for them now for the reconstruction of those roads and they are going to do it; but the end will be that the railroads, like the waterways, will be publicly owned. The great thing about a waterway is that it is like the King's highway. It is the people's road. The King's highway has never passed from the people; and the railways never should have passed from the people any more than the waterways have passed from them. In this new birth which is 'coming to America, which is coming very rapidly, the idea of newer and greater propositions in the way of transportation, in the way of developing power, in the way of using the national credit for the benefit of all the people and securing co-operative marketing -all these things will be taken up in the United States and in this country. And there will not be any trouble to get the money necessary to carry them out.
There is a lot of capital in the world which is ready to-day to foe invested in propositions of this kind. There will be no trouble in selling bonds. And no portion of Canada need fear this development. The Canadian Pacific Railway, even though it is located in Montreal, need not fear it. There will be all the railroad business which the Canadian Pacific Railway and the
National Railways can ever do in this country, even if they do have the competition of waterways. And the traffic will not move in one way. Traffic will come from Europe; return cargoes will come into our country. It may be of a nature that will make competition with our manufactures but they will have to accept that situation and adjust themselves to it. All the information that I have been able to gather, either by my reading or by talking to people, has led me to believe that the president and the government of the United States have struck the right idea. They are organized now to develop these things and to develop them immediately. Even if the money we need could not be found in this country the United States would perhaps be ready to be our bankers for a portion of the needed sum. But We do not need even to go to them for it

we can get our comparatively small portion of it in our own country and in Great Britain. I agree with my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) when he said that our portion will be a good deal less than one-half; the Americans have already admitted that. I also agree with him when he says that we have not any exclusive control of the St. Lawrence river or the Great Lakes, and that these waterways belong to both countries. It is a good thing that such is the case. It will have a tendency to maintain good and friendly feelings between the two nations; it is a bond of friendship and not a cause of jealousy between them. It is also cause for congratulation to ourselves. I hope the House will continue to discuss this question session after session until we reach some conclusion. It is not going to be long until that time arrives. Pressure is at work in the United States for applying these two means of relief- transportation for the farmers of the West in both countries, and water-power to electrify the railways. These two things are so pressing and so great that I have no doubt the necessary legislation, either in that country or this country, will be forthcoming at a very early date.
It was not hard to put the Panama canal scheme through the Congress of the United States. When they once took hold of it in earnest they soon accomplished it. As I said, the project has not brought results as quickly as was anticipated but it has given the United States the control of navigation in a surprising way. They are dominating the American continent to-day and the American continent above all others is our continent. We are an American
St. Lawrence Waterway

people but we are of British tendencies and believe in our own system of government. There is no reason for jealousy between us and the United States. Each of us can work out our own destiny whether it be in transportation or economic issues, and if we do that we will have no reason to regret it. We have had occasions in the past to disagree with the United States, and have had one or two small wars with them; but now the whole sentiment of that country is for our co-operation in a continental way, to develop these waterways just as they have developed their own. They have been somewhat misled by trusting too much to railways in the past but now they are coming back to waterways; and I have no doubt that before they are through the American government will own their own railroads just as we are finding we have got to own the railroads in this country. That does not mean any disadvantage to the Canadian Pacific railway, even though it is a company owned enterprise it will have to adjust itself to the new condition of affairs.
It is with pleasure and with a keen sense of duty that I intend to vote for the present resolution and to argue in favour of it on every occasion that may present itself. As I said before, I hope this discussion will not end now. I hope our friends from the West will assist in the improvement of these waterways just as the American farmers began to do when they realized the importance of them. If there is a Farmers' bloc in the United States there is also perhaps a Farmers' bloc in this House. I am glad to realize that our farmers are imbued with the idea of progress, that they have come here with the idea of assisting in the solution of these problems. The best way to solve such problems is by the nation working them out rather than individuals, that has been proved in the case of the development of power in Ontario. Power development has also been well worked out in Montreal by private companies; but in Ontario we are going to set an example to all the world in the development of waterpower for the people by the people, and to make that power as cheap as possible, not simply to realize profits for shareholders. It will be with some pride that we will be able to show that Ontario, under all the criticism that -has been passed by the men who favoured the private development of power, has worked this project out thoroughly and is making a successful use of the power developed. I make this prediction: that within ten years every rail-

road in Ontario-certainly from the Soo right across almost to Hudson bay-will be electrically equipped and will be able to carry freight at lower rates. The train services will be broken up into what I may term street car services. As to the passenger service, instead of there being three or four trains a day -between cities like Toronto and Montreal, or Ottawa and Montreal, cars will run at frequent intervals. They will run every hour, the speed will be greater, the service will be better and the cost much less. It will be economical, we will have improved service, our western plains will be filled up with farmers and that is what we want in this country. It will reduce the cost of transportation. Whether this scheme began with the United States or this country, it is now a continental scheme, bigger than Ontario and Quebec, and bigger than our East and West. It is as -big as the whole continent of North America, and the greatest continent in the world to-day is the North American continent. The richest valley in the world-and I do not like to have to say it-is the valley of the Mississippi, but we share largely in it, and we have our portion of it. The next greatest valley in the world is on the American continent, and it is the wheat valley of the Assiniboia and Saskatchewan. I believe the canalization of those valleys will come and the provinces in the West will soon have a great farming population, they will have reduced transportation rates, and we will soon get improved combinations for marketing.
That is the whole tendency of the discussion going on in Washington and in Canada, at the present time. That is why we have this talk of the Grain Growers, and why people in Canada say it is unconstitutional to have a grain board in Canada and that we cannot have it. But we will have a grain board, and the constitution and the lawyers will have to adjust themselves to it. That is one of the new signs of the times which have come into prominence since the war. The war is going to broaden the views of the nation and make the lawyers think differently. When law officers come to us and say we cannot have a wheat board and the farmers cannot organize a co-operative association, they cannot read the signs of the times. And this House will not read the signs of the times if it fails to do its share in the development of the St. Lawrence waterway for two great objects-the improvement of transportation and the devel-

St. Lawrence Waterway
opment oi water-power, not only for railways but for all the industries, for lighting the farmers' houses and driving their machinery.
All this is immediately in sight, because the simplicity of transmission of electrical energy has wonderfully improved. Hon. members may say I am a dreamer when I say that electrical energy will go through the air without wires, hut it is all coming. Did anybody ever believe two years ago that you would have seen this radio development? It is a mystery but it is there. It is going to make great changes in the world, but it will be for the benefit of humanity. I observe that the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) is in rather a humourous vain to-night, because he is smiling. The hon. Minister of War, as Peter Mitchell used to call him, will perhaps see that electrical energy, if war is to continue, will be of assistance. The greatest thing in the war-and it only came out in this war-was the radio wave, which transmitted some kind of energy through the air, and put an end to the war. It was a discovery the United States was able to disclose just at the end of the war, and it meant the destruction of scores of great warships by a man up in a balloon, directing by radio waves through the air attacks on warships. That is what put an end to the war, and that is the reason the navies have been scrapped. That is the real story of the war, it is coming out now, and I think the Minister of War will change his views somewhat. I do not know where the minister was at the time an effort was made to take away all the water-powers of the St. Lawrence and to give them to the Aluminum company of the United States, but thank goodness we have those great powers, and I hope we will keep them. While the United States have said in a way that they were against public ownership, they are going to have public ownership in the water-powers of the waters of the St. Lawrence. That is the greatest progress made in favour of public ownership.
What is that?

The United States to-day is developing these water-powers as a public ownership proposition for the electrical energy that can be developed by them. When somebody comes to me and tells me the United States are against public ownership, I will be able to cite that case. The United States has had to go to the assistance of the railways, in order to save them from absolute wreckage. The American railways are organizing themselves into ten or twelve regional systems and are going to the government to get the credit they require. They cannot find the money for the reconstruction of the roads, especially for their electrification.

The railroads were
ruined by public ownership during the war.
Which railroads?
The United States railways.
When?
During the war.

They were taken over by the United States during the war as a necessity.
Mr. 'BUREAU: And the United States ruined them.

And we ourselves have had to adopt public ownership. The hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) does not quite like the idea of pub-lice ownership. Would he like to see the King's highway go to private ownership. He does not like this new idea of the King's highway helping out the farmers to market, nor the idea of the public ownership of the waterways and the development of electrical energy, to be distributed to everybody at the cheapest possible price. It will not be ten years till electrical energy of some kind will be sent to every farm house in America. This is not a dream. The scientists are all working at it. When you see what they have done in the last two years by these radio waves, you will not have any doubt as to what the future is likely to be. The effect of the development of electrical energy by public ownership will be to increase the number of the common comforts of life, and to widen their distribution at the smallest possible cost. That is the theory of government ownership, I do not care how you put it. It is coming to the front very rapidly in Canada and the United States. I hope to see the day-and it will not be very long-when sufficient power will be generated right on our rivers to drive every train, not only in Quebec, but in Ontario. Sufficient power will be developed on the St. Lawrence and Niagara rivers to drive every train almost all over Canada, and to put cheap light and power in every house. It is coming.

St. Lawrence Waterway
The ground plan of the whole scheme is before us to-day in that report issued by this commission, and endorsed by President Harding, as he did the other day. As soon as he got the facts he went right to the people, and while the railroads have been able, by reason of their influence, to stop the discussion to some extent, the people are all thinking about it. The farm papers are all thinking about it, and the newspapers of the cities are coming to realize that their cities will all be greater, that if a city is greater on account of railroad development, it will be still greater when that railroad development is supplemented by the development of waterways and of electrical energy. Therefore, I am going to vote for this motion. There is going to be another election in this country-it may be soon or it may be some time off-but I am going to make a newer and broader national policy out of the development of our waterways in co-operation with the United States, if we can secure the cooperation of that country, or of a smaller development on our own account. We have started on our own account; we shall be able to improve the St. Lawrence and the Welland canal of our own motion, if we have to rely on ourselves, and it may be a good thing if we do this work ourselves. But I want to see it done for the benefit of this whole continent, as a great continental proposition, not as a national proposition in the United States or Canada; least of all do I want to see it discussed in this House from the point of view of provinces, or classes, or cities. America is great enough to take care of all our cities, of all our provinces, of all our peoples; and the greatest continent to-day and the one continent on which the hope of the world rests more than in any other country in the world is the continent of North America. That continent of North America happens to be possessed by us and our neighbours to the south of us. As my hon. friend opposite said, the United States and Canada have the same ideas in regard to government, and things economic, and we have no fear of the future. While Europe to-day is discouraged and broken into pieces by reason of racial and trade jealousies of one kind or another, there is a much better outlook for the whole North American continent and, I hope, also for the South American continent if we set the example. The beginning of this new development will be brought about by the cooperation of the United States and Canada 
for the development of the waterways of the St. Lawrence, and that proposition, which happens to be embodied in this resolution, is the greatest question that has ever come up in this Parliament of Canada.
May I ask a question of the hon. gentleman?
Yes, two, if my hon. friend so desires.
One is enough. Do I understand him to say that he suggests the development of the St. Lawrence river power by a partnership with the United States if we cannot do the work ourselves?

No, I said
that I should like to see it developed by both countries; but if it has to be done by us, we can develop it ourselves on a smaller scale. As the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) has said, we have the Welland canal under way now. Is my hon. friend opposite not prepared to co-operate with the United States in the development of the St. Lawrence?
I have no opinion to give. My hon. friend is advocating his side of the question.
The hon. member is a minister of the Crown, and I am sorry to see a minister of the Crown has not an opinion on this question.
I have an opinion, but I say I do not have to give it.
All right; keep it, and Heaven be with the hon. member while he has it. This Parliament must tackle this question and do something with it.

That does not answer
my question as regards a partnership with the United States in developing the St. Lawrence water-power.
I would not object to that, and I hope my hon. friend is in favour of the proposition of developing the St. Lawrence water-power.
Do not worry about me. Let the hon. member speak for himself.
I am speaking only for myself. Sir Wilfrid Laurier had no fear of joint action; I have no fear.

The hon. member had
-" No truck or trade with the Yankees."

St. Lawrence Waterway

That is a different question. The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in favour of co-operation in regard to the devlopment of the waterways of the St. Lawrence. Is my hon. friend in favour of the proposition? That is the question before the people of Canada.
I am not preaching the gospel. Let the hon. member give his own opinion.	,
I am giving mine. Will the hon. member kindly give his?
When the time comes, I will.

I am quite
sure my hon. friend will come to see this proposition in the same way that I see it, and he will see that his province and his great city of Montreal-
It is not mine.

-and I am not mentioning that city in any special way-will share in the development of Canada which will be brought about by the development of this waterway proposition to a greater extent than by any other proposition I have heard discussed in this House since I have been a member of it.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) is considering the proposition from one particular point of view. He is endeavouring to convince only one side of the House, and he turns always towards our good friends the Progressives. I had hoped, before he finished his argument, he would turn and appeal again to the whole House of Commons.
If I turned in that direction, I did not do so for the purpose my hon. friend suggests.

My hon. friend is perfectly right in doing that. I know that he tries to convince only one side of the House that he is afraid of; but those hon. members have already decided to vote in accordance with their own interests, and as regards the solution of the railway question, they will be satisfied without any St. Lawrence waterway.
As regards the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), everyone may have his own opinion. I know from his constituency, the hon. member for Welland lives on the
shores near the great Welland canal, and he is well aware that, if this proposed scheme were carried into effect, he would see transatlantic steamers passing the fine city of Toronto, going through the Welland canal, to ports on the upper lakes, Erie, Huron, Michigan, and Superior. Everybody in that part of the country would like to see those steamers go further, even to the ports of Detroit, Port Huron, Chicago, Port William and Port Arthur. It is the duty of the representatives of Ontario to advocate whatever is for the welfare of their province; they are entitled to vindicate their right and to do the best they can for their province. Everyone is entitled to work for his province and to make the best use of the opportunities he finds on the floor of this House to secure the passage of certain measures. We have the same aim in Quebec; but in doing all these things, we have only one thing in sight, namely the welfare of the whole of Canada. I hope I do not hurt the feelings of my good friend the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), who moved the resolution before the House' when I tell him that this is a dream, a' lovely dream. Conditions in Canada at the present time, if we disregard the financial situation which is pretty bad, are not worse and are, perhaps, better than those of any other country in the world. Our railways are practically in a stagnant condition, but, if we give them a fair trial, better days may come for them. Our trade is suffering somewhat on account of the aftermath of the war; but to bring back prosperity to trade and commerce, and to our factories, you do not need to develop the St. Lawrence waterway. You do not need to tamper with nature's creations and demolish the natural gifts which Providence ha's bestowed upon each province. Let us take them as we find them and make what use we can of them without encroaching, one province upon another. Let each province strive to obtain from its natural resources all the wealth that lies hidden therein; but do not let us interfere with the rights of others. I was somewhat surprised at the views expressed by my learned friend from South York (Mr. Maclean).
Not learned.
My hon. friend has much learning.

And by the time this session is over I predict that he will be still more learned. The hon. member is

I was going to say, as the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) remarked a moment ago, that in 1911 the Conservative members from Toronto-perhaps not the same gentlemen who actually represent that city in the House of Commons to-day, at any rate, members of the same political persuasion, the same policy, and animated with the same spirit-were not so very eulogistic of the United States and its enterprises.
